title: Documentation home
summary: 1 · Visual C · Stage 1 In one sentence: Visual C runs a C program under a debugger, saves what it saw into a file (a trace), and lets other code read that file safely. The big picture C files + build options │ ▼ ┌─────────────────
text: 1 · Visual C · Stage 1 In one sentence: Visual C runs a C program under a debugger, saves what it saw into a file (a trace), and lets other code read that file safely. The big picture C files + build options │ ▼ ┌───────────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ ┌───────────────────┐ │ Trace Engine │ ─────► │ trace.json │ ─────► │ Trace Parser │ ─► your code │ compile + record │ │ (saved run) │ │ load + check + ask│ └───────────────────┘ └──────────────┘ └───────────────────┘ THE CAMERA THE VIDEO THE VIEWER {{diagram:architecture}} Think of it as a scientific recording. The program runs once while a tool collects evidence. Afterwards, readers ask questions of the saved evidence. They do not re-run the experiment. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Trace The saved record of one run of a C program. It lists what was captured and what could not be captured. Stage 1 The first half of Visual C: compile, run under a debugger, record, export, then load and check. The later "semantic engine" (Stage 2) is a separate layer not covered here. Trace Engine The recording side. It compiles the program, runs a bounded debugger session (limited in time, steps and memory) and writes a version-2 JSON trace. Trace Parser The reading side. It loads the JSON so other code can inspect the records without changing them. Checkpoint A selected pause in the run where variables and memory were read. Gap An interval of execution that was not recorded exactly. Validated The records passed extra consistency checks. It does not mean every moment of execution was seen. The central idea: observation is not conclusion A debugger can only say "at this pause, these bytes were readable." That is useful, but on its own it cannot tell you more. The debugger showed… You can say You cannot say (from that alone) --------- Four bytes for variable sum at a pause Those four bytes were readable then sum was initialized earlier (it could be leftover garbage) A pointer holding 0x1000 The pointer held that address The pointer came from allocation 7 A complete log from the followed process That process's allocator calls were seen Every child process was observed Visual C records the observation and the uncertainty around it. As a reader, hold on to two habits: 1. Keep addresses separate from identities(schema.htmlidentity-domains). An address is just a place in memory, and a later allocation can reuse it. 2. Tell apart a structurally sound trace from a complete execution(parser-validation.htmllevel-2-architecture). "The file is consistent" and "we saw everything" are different claims. What ships Tool Role in Stage 1 ------ GCC Compiles your C code into a runnable program. GDB Runs the program and pauses it so values can be read. DWARF Debug information stored inside the compiled program; describes types and source lines. Allocator wrapper Records memory calls (malloc, free, …) that it can intercept. Clang (optional) Reads the source text and describes it. Valgrind / sanitizers Memory-error checkers that run in other executions, so their findings are not allocation IDs from the GDB run. One saved trace(model.html) holds: selected pauses (checkpoints), attempted instructions, missing intervals (gaps), observed heap lifetimes (when each allocation was created and freed), and diagnostic reports. The Trace Engine(engine-build.html) writes it. The Trace Parser(parser-ingestion.html) reads the final JSON once, builds lookup tables of positions, and returns references to the saved items, a validation report, and pages of results. Asking a new question never rewrites earlier observations. Choose your route If you want to… Start with ------ Follow the whole run Complete pipeline(pipeline.html) → Engine architecture(engine-architecture.html) → Parser architecture(parser-architecture.html) → Debugger lifecycle(engine-debugger.html) Navigate unfamiliar code Source files(files.html), functions and types(functions.html), module relationships(dependencies.html), call-flow explorer(call-flow.html) Add an engine feature Compilation(engine-build.html), variable capture(engine-memory.html), heap telemetry(engine-heap.html) (allocation recording), budgets(engine-limits.html) Consume evidence Parser ingestion(parser-ingestion.html), validation(parser-validation.html), semantic confidence(parser-semantic.html), bounded pages(parser-consumer.html), Stage 2 handoff(handoff.html) Look up a type Public API(api.html), schema and identity tables(schema.html), the page outline, or offline search (press /) Where to begin in code Purpose Location ------ Recording entry point src/trace.rs::trace_program(TraceConfig) Saved data shape src/models.rs::DebugSessionTrace Parser entry point src/trace_parser/mod.rs::TraceStore::open Deeper validation TraceStore::validated_semantic() in semantic.rs Stable consumer example examples/stage1_public_consumer_audit.rs (runnable intro in Practical usage(usage.html)) Scope and inspected version Inspected version: base revision 558037c0da180e152a3e6cc3f351edf0b0583215 plus existing uncommitted Stage 1 changes. The commit hash alone does not identify the inspected parser sources. See the repository map(repository.html) and DOC-1 report(DOC1-REPORT.md). Important: The Stage 1 freeze is approved within a bounded evidence scope. It is not a sandbox, a whole-process-tree tracer, a memory-initialization oracle, or a guarantee about assembled-trace RAM. See the precise limits(handoff.htmlknown-limitations). This site explains Stage 1, including the final realloc repair. It is not a manual for Stage 2 internals. Using this site offline Open index.html in a browser. Search, diagrams, themes, navigation and content are all local, so no network is needed. The README(README.md) explains regeneration; every generated page is checked in next to its Markdown source.

title: How to read this reference
summary: 2 · How to read this reference In one sentence: Don't read in order. Start with a question, find the page that answers it, and only then open the code. Pick a starting point Your question Go to ------ "How does a program turn into
text: 2 · How to read this reference In one sentence: Don't read in order. Start with a question, find the page that answers it, and only then open the code. Pick a starting point Your question Go to ------ "How does a program turn into a trace?" Complete pipeline(pipeline.html) "What is this type or function?" Function index(functions.html), then the call-flow explorer(call-flow.html) "Where does this file/directory fit?" Repository map(repository.html), Source file index(files.html) "What does this recorded value mean?" Identity contracts(identity-contracts.html) "Why is an allocation missing?" Heap overview → event-reader links → coverage links → compare with the actual trace Example. To find why an allocation is missing, follow that last route and then compare with the real trace file. Finding a record with a matching address is not an answer, because addresses are reused. What an index entry does and doesn't tell you An index/graph entry… Means Does not mean --------- Lists a file or definition The code exists at that path It ran in any particular recording Was found by a script A real Rust/C definition at a real location A verified call, or a written explanation of its algorithm Appears as a graph edge Someone read the production caller and callee — (edges are published only after this check) Is labeled "conceptual" It explains the architecture A runtime function call For deeper reading, the DOC-2 engine chapters and DOC-3 parser chapters include source-guided walkthroughs, branches and error paths. Use the navigation to open them. Version this reference describes This is a map of the inspected working tree (the folder of code as it was on disk), not of a commit alone. - Base revision: 558037c0da180e152a3e6cc3f351edf0b0583215 - The parser and its tests had uncommitted changes at inspection time. - Line numbers refer to that state and can shift as the repository changes. Navigating offline - Sidebar, breadcrumbs, outline, previous/next all work from checked-in HTML. - Search uses a generated local JavaScript index (no fetch), covering source paths and symbol names. - Source links in a file:// browser open a local repository file. The adjacent path:line text gives the exact location even if the browser can't jump to the line. - The maintenance guide(README.md) explains regeneration. Read evidence before inference Keep these five layers separate in your mind: Layer Example of confusing it with another --------- 1 The recorded execution — 2 Static source metadata A syntax match is not an executed expression 3 Independent diagnostics (other runs) An address match is not a lifetime identity 4 Validation findings A successful import is not semantic validation 5 Downstream interpretation — The limitations page(limitations.html) is part of every walkthrough, not an appendix to skip.

title: What Stage 1 does
summary: 3 · Architecture · one recording, many qualified readers In one sentence: The engine records, the parser reads, and every kind of evidence is kept labeled with what it can and cannot prove. Level 1 · Intuition Imagine recording a
text: 3 · Architecture · one recording, many qualified readers In one sentence: The engine records, the parser reads, and every kind of evidence is kept labeled with what it can and cannot prove. Level 1 · Intuition Imagine recording a short video of a C program and giving it to someone who wasn't there. - The Trace Engine is the camera. It compiles the program, runs it under a debugger, and saves the moments it actually observed. - The Trace Parser is the viewer. It opens the finished recording and helps other code find moments in it. The viewer can't ask the finished program what happened between two recorded moments. That's why the trace also records gaps: the places where the camera wasn't looking. The recording is a JSON file, and parser queries point back to its original observations rather than changing it. {{diagram:architecture}} Level 2 · Pipeline and boundaries The tools, in plain words Tool / term What it is Important limit --------- GCC The C compiler — Debug executable A compiled program with extra info for debuggers; the engine also links an allocation logger into it — DWARF The debug-info format inside that executable Describes the compiled result; gives no value for every variable at every moment Clang AST (optional) A tree Clang builds from the source text (it can spot the written malloc(40)) Text presence does not show the call ran GDB The debugger that runs and pauses the executable Sees pauses, not the time between MI2 GDB's machine-readable command format, so the engine can ask for a frame or variable automatically — Inferior The program GDB is debugging A followed inferior is observed; a forked child it doesn't follow gets no automatic snapshots What happens, in order Step What happens --------- 1 Configure and build A TraceConfig names the C files, program arguments, and time/memory/recording limits. GCC builds the debug program and may try a second build with a sanitizer (compiler-inserted checks for buffer overflows, use-after-free, etc.). If compilation fails, the result holds compiler errors, not imaginary snapshots. 2 Read types, then observe The engine reads DWARF. If requested, Clang examines the source. GDB runs the program and pauses it at selected stops. A stop is a moment we can ask "what does this variable look like right now?" 3 Log allocations A wrapper around malloc, free, etc. acts as a detour: the call reaches the wrapper, which logs it and then calls the real allocator. Each line carries a PID (which process) and a sequence number (order within that process). The engine reads new lines at each stop. The log goes to its own file, never mixed into the program's output. 4 Package and export Observations become one DebugSessionTrace, exported as JSON. A JSONL journal (one small JSON record per line) may be written along the way; it helps keep a partial run but can't rebuild the final document. 5 Load and read TraceStore::open loads the JSON and builds position lookups. Loading only says the file has a supported shape. Call validated_semantic() to check consistency. Queries return references to original records, in pages of at most 128 records. {{diagram:compilation}} Three runs that must not be mixed up Run What executes Reports Can supply Run 1 allocation IDs? ------------ Run 1 · primary Debug executable under GDB Stopped variables and heap events with IDs like "allocation 17" Yes (via its own wrapper) Run 2 · if enabled Separately built sanitizer executable Memory problems caught by compiler-added checks No Run 3 · if enabled Valgrind on another execution (no sanitizer build needed) Invalid memory operations, leaks No Each run has its own status: succeeded, failed or skipped. Example. Valgrind reports "40 leaked bytes at line 52." That's useful, but it does not prove the leaked block is allocation 17 from Run 1, since addresses and allocation order can differ between runs. What each evidence provider can and cannot prove Provider Can tell you Cannot prove by itself --------- GCC and DWARF How the compiled program describes types, declarations, source lines Which expressions ran, or what a variable held later GDB/MI State at a recorded pause, including bounded reads Anything between pauses, or an unfollowed child's state C allocation wrapper Calls it intercepted in the primary run, with PID, order, ID Allocations made wholly inside unwrapped shared libraries Optional Clang AST Code that appears in the source, and where That an expression executed Valgrind / sanitizers Errors in their own executions The exact primary-run allocation ID of an error Level 3 · Trace through the implementation Start at src/trace.rs::trace_program. In order, it: 1. checks ExecutionLimits, 2. starts a supervised session, 3. calls compiler::compile_project to build the program, 4. extracts DWARF with dwarf::extract_excluding, and 5. runs clang_ast::analyze only if configured. The stop loop uses src/gdb_mi.rs, src/recorder.rs and src/allocation_tracker.rs. src/models.rs defines the saved data; src/json_export.rs writes it. On the reading side, src/trace_parser/mod.rs::TraceStore::assemble keeps one shared Arc<DebugSessionTrace plus position indexes. Arc is Rust's shared-ownership handle: many readers share one trace without copying its records. rust // Core architecture signatures; source: src/trace.rs and src/trace_parser. pub async fn trace_program(config: TraceConfig) - Result<DebugSessionTrace; // TraceStore's public entry point (method declaration): pub fn open(path: impl AsRef<Path, options: TraceLoadOptions) - Result<Self; // Constructing this view runs one opt-in validation pass: pub fn validated_semantic(&self) - ValidatedSemanticView<'_; Note: These are signature excerpts, not one runnable file; each lives in its own module. See practical usage(usage.html) for a working program. Four questions to ask at every boundary Before treating two facts as one story, ask: - Did GDB observe this? - Is it only a description of the source? - Did it come from another run? - Is it a parser warning or a later interpretation? For instance, a pointer holding an address and an allocation recorded at that address are two separate observations. Evidence confidence(parser-semantic.html) shows how the parser keeps them apart.

title: Complete pipeline
summary: 4 · Complete Stage 1 pipeline In one sentence: One C program goes from source files to a saved recording, then a reader opens that recording. The parser never runs C code and can't fill in missing observations. The key distinction
text: 4 · Complete Stage 1 pipeline In one sentence: One C program goes from source files to a saved recording, then a reader opens that recording. The parser never runs C code and can't fill in missing observations. The key distinction throughout: what the program did in the main debugger run versus what another tool found in a separate run. The system boundary {{diagram:stage1-system}} Part A · Recording (Trace Engine) Step 1 — Build a program we can inspect Piece What it does ------ GCC Builds a debug executable: a program with extra info so GDB can link machine instructions to source lines, types and variables. DWARF That extra info. It describes the compiled program, not a history of what happened when it ran. Allocation logger Built in with --wrap, a linker option that redirects calls (see below). Sanitizer build GCC attempts a second executable with sanitizer checks. It may fail or be skipped without erasing the debug run's observations. Clang AST (optional) A structured outline of written expressions. An entry for malloc(40) is a clue about the source, not evidence the call happened. How --wrap works. The linker option --wrap=malloc redirects calls so they pass through the project's own function first: your code calls: malloc(40) │ ▼ __wrap_malloc(40) ← the project's wrapper: writes a log entry │ ("this run allocated 40 bytes") ▼ __real_malloc(40) ← the real allocator, reached through the linker calloc, realloc and free are wrapped the same way, and your C source doesn't change. The limit: only calls it intercepts are recorded. Allocations made entirely inside unwrapped libraries aren't promised. Step 2 — Observe the primary run Piece What it does ------ GDB Runs the debug executable. MI2 GDB's machine-readable language: "continue," "stop," "show me this variable." Inferior The program being debugged. The engine observes its followed inferior, not every process created by fork. Stop A pause where variables and memory can be read. New wrapper log lines are read at every stop. PID + sequence number Each log line says which process wrote it and its order within that process. The wrapper log is a separate file so allocator messages can't be confused with the program's normal output. And a child process or instruction that was never observed doesn't become a fact just because a later stop was captured. Step 3 — Keep separate runs separate Run Executable Status --------- Run 1 · primary Debug executable under GDB Own status Run 2 · sanitizer (if enabled) Separate sanitizer executable Own status Run 3 · Valgrind (if enabled) Another execution Own status Statuses are completed, failed or skipped. Runs 2 and 3 can report useful errors such as "40 bytes leaked near line 52." They can't reliably say "that was allocation 17 in Run 1," since a new run may use different addresses or allocate in a different order. Only Run 1's wrapper events supply Run 1's allocation IDs. Reading the diagram's arrows Arrow Meaning ------ Solid A tool produces an artifact or passes actual runtime data. Dashed Optional, independent or only a possible match. It does not mean Clang or Valgrind observed the GDB execution. See Trace Engine architecture(engine-architecture.html) for control flow and evidence contracts(identity-contracts.html) for what each tool can prove. Part B · Handoff and reading {{diagram:engine-parser-flow}} Stage What happens What it does not do --------- Package Observations gather into a DebugSessionTrace (defined in src/models.rs). — Export src/json_export.rs writes it as JSON. — Journal (during recording) JSONL writes records one per line and can preserve a partial run. It is not a full replacement for the final JSON; it lacks some final reports and reconstructed state. Load TraceStore::open keeps one canonical shared copy and builds small lookup tables. A successful load says the schema is supported. It does not prove records agree with each other. Validate Call validated_semantic() before relying on relationships such as "this realloc came from that earlier allocation." The parser never restarts GDB or changes history. Where to continue - Inside the recording: engine architecture(engine-architecture.html) - How loading avoids copying per query: parser ownership(parser-architecture.html) - Individual implementations: source file index(files.html) - New to PID, allocation ID, checkpoint or EvidenceRef? Keep the glossary(glossary.html) open alongside.

title: Trace Engine architecture
summary: 5 · Trace Engine architecture In one sentence: The engine is a coordinator. It asks several smaller parts to compile, observe, record and export, then assembles the result. Two terms first Term Meaning ------ Supervisor Sets deadl
text: 5 · Trace Engine architecture In one sentence: The engine is a coordinator. It asks several smaller parts to compile, observe, record and export, then assembles the result. Two terms first Term Meaning ------ Supervisor Sets deadlines and manages child tool processes, so a hung compiler or debugger can't run forever unnoticed. Subsystem A group of related source files. Example: gdb_mi talks to GDB; recorder saves what was observed. What happens at one pause When GDB pauses, the engine: 1. checks why it stopped, 2. collects the current frame (the executing function and its local variables), 3. reads new allocator log lines, and 4. saves a snapshot. Later, it may run a sanitizer in a separate execution. Don't assume: A diagram of the normal route does not promise every optional tool ran, or that every instruction between two stops was seen. The engine can pause and inspect at selected moments only. It can't fill in unseen time or unknown child processes afterwards. Entry points: trace::trace_program arranges timeouts and cleanup, trace_program_inner organizes the work, and run_gdb_phase handles the debugger. Subsystems, as a journey {{diagram:engine-subsystems}} Order Module Job --------- 1 cli, config Turn your command into a request 2 supervisor, resource_limits Watch time and other limits 3 compiler Ask GCC to build the debug program (including the C allocation wrapper) and report compiler errors 4 gdb_mi, mi_parser Send commands to GDB / translate GDB's text replies into fields 5 recorder, storage Remember pauses and attempted instructions / write a bounded JSONL journal 6 allocation_tracker Turn wrapper log lines into recorded heap events 7 dwarf, clang_ast (optional), evidence Link records to type or source descriptions, only when a match is justified 8 valgrind, sanitizer Handle the other runs 9 models, json_export Define the result / write the final JSON Reminder: a pointer's address matching an allocation's address is not that pointer's allocation history. Inside the stop loop At a pause, GDB reports the address of the instruction the program is about to execute. The loop then: 1. reads new output and wrapper events, 2. finds out why the program paused, 3. captures current state within its budgets, and 4. decides how to continue. Two GDB messages look alike but differ: "I accepted your continue command" is not "the program stopped again." If the loop skips an interval inside a library or wrapper, it records a gap rather than inventing instruction records. More: debugger chapter(engine-debugger.html) (step-by-step example), call-flow explorer(call-flow.html) (checked code paths). Runtime order and conditionals {{diagram:runtime-lifecycle}} The diagram is an overview; not every optional pass always runs at one fixed point. Situation What happens ------ Sanitizer trigger already met The sanitizer pass can run before Valgrind Trigger not yet met The Valgrind result may decide whether the sanitizer runs After runtime and heap records are assembled DWARF association and evidence fusion (linking records from different providers, only where justified) Clang configured Clang extraction runs (it's optional) Compilation fails A trace with diagnostics is returned, with no GDB observations See src/trace.rs and process boundaries(resource-boundaries.html) for exact branches. Follow the implementation Location What happens there ------ src/main.rs:34 Calls trace::trace_program src/trace.rs:132 Supervises the session src/trace.rs:167 Orchestrates it src/trace.rs:1113 Begins the debugger phase The source index lists all files. Function-to-function call claims belong in the verified explorer, not in arrows inferred between module names.

title: Trace Parser architecture
summary: 6 · Trace Parser architecture In one sentence: The parser works after recording. It makes a saved trace safe and convenient to inspect without pretending it can watch the program again. Two terms first Term Meaning ------ Deserial
text: 6 · Trace Parser architecture In one sentence: The parser works after recording. It makes a saved trace safe and convenient to inspect without pretending it can watch the program again. Two terms first Term Meaning ------ Deserialize Turn JSON text into Rust records. Proves the file is readable in the expected format, not that its claims agree. Validate Check relationships between records (e.g. does a claimed realloc predecessor have supporting events?). Example. A JSON file says old_id=7, but event 7 was a different allocation. Loading succeeds because the field is well-formed. Deep validation rejects the unsupported relationship. The parser answers questions about a recorded trace without rebuilding or silently correcting it. It does not guess which record the author meant. Its store is immutable (nothing changes after loading), and queries borrow the original records: you get a reference, not a copy. Positions in compact indexes point back into one canonical Arc<DebugSessionTrace. Loading is not validating {{diagram:parser-subsystems}} File Job ------ json.rs Selects and decodes supported schema-v2 JSON journal.rs Handles ordered JSONL records separately mod.rs Constructs TraceStore indexes.rs Builds position-based lookups instead of cloning records views.rs Exposes raw and borrowed views evidence.rs Checks trace-scoped references validation.rs Opt-in checks; can report a trace as structurally unsound, partial, or having an unavailable relationship semantic.rs Confidence-qualified evidence via validated_semantic() consumer.rs Bounded checkpoint pages (up to 128 entries per request) Name clash: trace_parser/semantic.rs is a Stage 1 evidence interface. It is not the excluded Stage 2 src/semantic/ module. Imported trace ownership {{diagram:ownership}} - Cloning a TraceStore shares its trace and indexes through Arc, so a clone is cheap. - A second, independently loaded copy of an identical JSON document is a different owner. - An EvidenceRef (a citation pointing to one record) is valid only against the store that issued it. Another store's numeric positions don't become valid references. Memory notes: - Index memory estimates are not the parser process's RSS (memory the process actually holds), and not a cap on whole-trace RAM. - The exporter's cap applies to each written JSON document, not to an assembled trace in memory. The realloc repair (TP8-F01) ------ Found by The historical TP-8 audit (a review of the parser) Problem A forged realloc predecessor could be reported with Definite confidence (the strongest level) even though nothing supported it Fix TP8-F01 changed deep validation and semantic confidence Now required Compatible recorded realloc events and lifetime boundaries from the same PID Unchanged Raw imported fields are still preserved; schema-only loading is still allowed Reading order: deep validation(parser-validation.html) → confidence(parser-semantic.html) → the approved Stage 1 audit(../stage1-final-audit.md). The older conditional TP-8 report predates the repair. Next implementation path Start at src/trace_parser/mod.rs, then json.rs, indexes.rs, views.rs, validation.rs. The function index(functions.html) also lists private parsers and helpers. The DOC-3 parser handbook(parser-handbook.html) already explains their control flow in more detail.

title: Evidence and identity contracts
summary: 7 · Evidence and identity contracts In one sentence: A trace is full of numbers, and they are not interchangeable just because they print the same. Two terms first Term Meaning ------ Identity domain What a number identifies: a de
text: 7 · Evidence and identity contracts In one sentence: A trace is full of numbers, and they are not interchangeable just because they print the same. Two terms first Term Meaning ------ Identity domain What a number identifies: a debugger stop, an array position, a process, a heap lifetime. Each has its own rules. Provenance Evidence of where a pointer actually came from, which is more than "which recorded block contains this address." Example. A block at 0x1000 is freed, and a different block is later allocated at 0x1000. The address matches, but the wrapper gives the two lifetimes different IDs. A pointer holding 0x1000 doesn't tell us which lifetime produced it. Likewise, a matching source line or value from a Valgrind run is a possible clue, not proof of a link to the main debugger run. Evidence can't be made more certain by reusing a number from the wrong domain. Stage 1 keeps four things distinct, each with its own identities: the stopped execution, the retained recording, static metadata, and separate diagnostic runs. Identity domains {{diagram:identity-domains}} This… …is not the same as Because --------- Snapshot vector position GDB stop ID Different counters Attempted instruction Retained instruction-event position Retention and gaps are accounted separately Frame activation (one call of a function) A variable's address Different things PID-local allocation event / trace-local lifetime ID A numeric address They're linked by recorded wrapper events and reconstructable boundaries DWARF declaration/type IDs AST declaration/expression IDs Two separate static providers A TraceStore position A valid reference elsewhere References also require the same canonical trace owner Matching source site (file + line) Exact same-execution allocation identity At best a candidate Facts, candidates and unknowns Evidence Supported interpretation Unsupported promotion --------- GDB stop and bounded read Observed stopped-state bytes/status Initialized C object, or every intermediate instruction DWARF DIE and optional AST node Compiled metadata or source syntax Proof that a syntax node executed Wrapper event and same-PID lifetime Observed interceptor event and qualified predecessor Origin inferred from a reused address Valgrind/ASan report Independent diagnostic Primary-run allocation ID from matching line/address Complete observed-PID heap history Verified scope of seen PIDs and the followed inferior Census of silent fork descendants A DIE is one entry in the DWARF data. ASan is AddressSanitizer, the common sanitizer for memory errors. Silent fork descendants are child processes that produced no wrapper events. Provenance at the public boundary {{diagram:public-consumer}} Check ValidationReport::is_structurally_sound() separately from whether the trace is partial. validated_semantic() borrows the store and labels each relationship with one of five confidence levels: Level Meaning ------ Definite Verified for a specific observation, within its documented scope Candidate Compatible evidence, but unproved Ambiguous Several relationships fit Unavailable Not enough evidence Contradictory Structurally rejected A contradiction doesn't erase the raw record. Missing evidence is never converted into a negative fact. Bounded consumer pages expose the original trace-scoped references, and Stage 1 intentionally ends there. Read next When an identity looks obvious from printed addresses alone, check schema and identity reference(schema.html), parser validation(parser-validation.html) and limitations(limitations.html) first.

title: Process and resource boundaries
summary: 8 · Process and resource boundaries In one sentence: Different limits protect different stages. A cap on what's written to a file is not a cap on what the process holds in memory. The caps at a glance Limit Controls Does not contr
text: 8 · Process and resource boundaries In one sentence: Different limits protect different stages. A cap on what's written to a file is not a cap on what the process holds in memory. The caps at a glance Limit Controls Does not control --------- Journal cap Max size of the JSONL record stream written while tracing The final JSON document Export cap Max size of one final JSON document written out The already-built trace sitting in RAM Parser input / page limits What the parser accepts and returns (TP-7 rejects pages wider than 128 rather than truncating) The engine's export setting; process RSS Resource controls overall Accidental runaway work A hostile program (not a sandbox) Example. A 2 KB journal can stop growing while the final JSON still takes 22 KB. That's expected: they are different products with different caps, and the missing journal tail must stay visible. The engine limits a collection session, the journal and the export independently. The parser has its own input/page limits and validation findings. None of this implies a hostile-code sandbox, and none bounds all assembled Rust objects. Who enforces what {{diagram:resource-failure}} Layer Enforces ------ supervisor A whole-session monotonic deadline (clock that never jumps backwards) and child-process cleanup resource_limits Supported process restrictions; process-count limits use cgroups (a Linux feature for limiting process resources) only where available GDB stop loop Budgets for steps, instructions, commands, snapshots, variables and memory reads Recorder / storage Journal limits on JSONL records json_export A separate per-document byte cap on the final JSON What happens on failure: a timeout or limit may retain a partial trace. An export failure is an operational error and is not a successful exported trace. Two different completeness questions execution_status, stage_results, gaps and process/heap coverage each answer a different question: - A stage can fail after some records were captured. - A debugger can stop at a limit without proving the C program would never terminate. - A heap event transport or ACK (acknowledgement message) failure shrinks the verified observed-PID history. - Even a complete observed-PID history says nothing about a child that produced no event. The parser reports these distinctions and does not fill them in. Parser and consumer limits - The parser rejects oversized input independently of the engine's export setting. - It does not reconstruct final trace state from JSONL. - Validation can call a trace structurally sound but partial, or mark one relationship unavailable. Concrete settings: engine limits(engine-limits.html) and the parser API(api.html). Security scope Warning: These controls protect against accidental runaway work. They do not protect the host against an adversarial executable. For hostile C programs, use external OS or container isolation. Read the actual resource and process modules before changing any cleanup assumptions.

title: Repository map
summary: 9 · Repository map In one sentence: A map from "what do I want to know?" to "which directory answers it?" You don't need to memorize the repository. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Production source The Rust and C code that actually
text: 9 · Repository map In one sentence: A map from "what do I want to know?" to "which directory answers it?" You don't need to memorize the repository. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Production source The Rust and C code that actually performs recording or parsing, as opposed to tests or generated HTML pages. Fixture A small example C program used by tests to check one behavior. How the crate is organized The project is one Rust package with one CLI binary and one library target. Stage 1 is not split into separate engine and parser packages. The two halves share the trace model (models) as their common wire contract: the engine writes it, the parser reads it. Out of scope: Stage 2's src/semantic/ lives in the same crate but is outside this documentation inventory. Production directories Directory Responsibility Start here --------- src/ CLI, session orchestration, models, debugger, metadata, diagnostics, limits and export Engine architecture(engine-architecture.html) src/evidence/ Post-processing links between existing provider records, without turning syntax into execution Metadata chapter(engine-metadata.html) src/trace_parser/ Schema ingestion, immutable indexes, borrowed views, opt-in validation, qualified evidence and pages Parser architecture(parser-architecture.html) c_runtime/ The C allocator wrapper that is compiled and linked into the debug executable Heap chapter(engine-heap.html) tests/ Rust integration tests and adversarial regression tests Source file index(files.html) fixtures/c/ C programs used as observable test subjects Practical usage(usage.html) examples/ CLI outputs, audit probes and reference consumers API reference(api.html) Where the project touches the outside world Visual C talks to other programs. These are subprocess boundaries (separate programs communicating through files or pipes), not Rust modules calling each other in-process. External piece How it's used ------ Cargo.toml Describes the Rust package and its libraries src/config.rs Models the build and runtime requests GCC Builds the target binaries GDB/MI2 Communicates through a tokened process protocol (messages carry a token so replies can be matched to requests) addr2line May resolve which source location a caller address belongs to Clang (optional) Produces syntax metadata Valgrind Emits its own separate XML diagnostics Sanitizer binaries Emit their own separate reports Example route: from C allocation to trace record To understand how a C allocation becomes a trace record, read in this order: 1. c_runtime/alloc_tracker.c (the C wrapper that logs the call) 2. src/allocation_tracker.rs (Rust side that turns log lines into events) 3. the heap parser chapters (how the saved events are read back) A file's presence doesn't mean its optional feature ran in every trace. Check the recording's stage statuses too. Navigate by relationship {{diagram:module-dependencies}} Module-level arrows show data or compile-time dependencies. They do not claim that every named function calls another module's function. For… Use ------ Direct calls Call-flow explorer(call-flow.html) All definitions and their locations Function index(functions.html) Machine-readable data The inventory(assets/data/stage1-inventory.json), which can later be extended with carefully verified edges Which version is documented The source state is base commit 558037c0da180e152a3e6cc3f351edf0b0583215 plus pre-existing uncommitted changes. The commit alone does not reproduce the parser's TP-6/7 and TP8-F01 implementation as inspected. See the DOC-1 report(DOC1-REPORT.md) for exact scope and caveats.

title: Source file index
summary: 10 · Source file index In one sentence: A table of contents for the actual source tree. A path tells you where an implementation lives, not that it ran. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Generated catalog A listing built by scanning t
text: 10 · Source file index In one sentence: A table of contents for the actual source tree. A path tells you where an implementation lives, not that it ran. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Generated catalog A listing built by scanning the current source tree, so you can navigate even when a file has no long explanation yet. Source location A file and line number where a definition can be read. The number may shift after code edits. Example. Searching src/gdb_mi.rs helps you find the debugger commands. It does not show a particular command ran in your trace. That needs recorded evidence. What's listed - Every Stage 1 Rust file under src/ - The allocator wrapper under c_runtime/ - Not src/semantic/ (deliberately excluded; it's Stage 2) File names, paths and symbols come from the checked-in, generated, machine-readable inventory. Each file's short responsibility note describes a subsystem. It is not a replacement for reading the implementation. Browsing the catalog Select a file to open its source, or follow its symbol count to the function index(functions.html). Line locations refer to the inspected working tree. Tip: Local browsers may open the source file but ignore the line number. The adjacent path:line text is the reliable locator. Stage 1 file catalog {{inventory:files}} How far to trust this list Question Answer ------ How is the list checked? Against repository file discovery, not an old design document. Are definitions and module references verified calls? No. They're labeled as automatically discovered in the JSON. Where are verified execution edges? Maintained separately in the call-flow dataset(call-flow.html). Do adjacent file names form a call chain? No. For how files cooperate, use the walkthroughs. Are there fuller explanations? Yes. Follow the DOC-2 engine handbook and DOC-3 parser handbook for the existing implementation walkthroughs in this same website.

title: Function index
summary: 11 · Function and type index In one sentence: An address book for code names. It is not a list of functions your program executed. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Definition The place in a Rust or C file where a function or type is
text: 11 · Function and type index In one sentence: An address book for code names. It is not a list of functions your program executed. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Definition The place in a Rust or C file where a function or type is declared. Call-flow link A separate, reviewed arrow showing that one piece of code calls another, transfers data, or marks a conceptual boundary. Example. Look up validate_deep here to open its source. Then read the validation chapter to learn why it distinguishes a corrupt trace from a partial one. What this index is (and isn't) It covers production Stage 1 definitions, including important private helpers. For each, it gives the signature and source location as a starting point. It is It is not ------ A lookup of names, signatures and locations A story of how a function gets invoked Searchable by qualified name, type or path An explanation of each algorithm An address book alongside the DOC-2/DOC-3 chapters Proof of a runtime call Why it can't prove calls: source parsing alone can't see dispatch through traits (Rust's interfaces), callbacks, or another process. Browsing Use the local search with a qualified function name, type or source path. Expand a symbol to see its signature and source reference. - For selected verified callers and callees, open the call-flow explorer(call-flow.html). - Functions not connected in the curated graph are still listed here. See the existing engine handbook(engine-handbook.html) and parser handbook(parser-handbook.html) for longer explanations. Source locations {{inventory:functions}} Template for future function walkthroughs A later, full walkthrough of one function must cover these ten points. Line-by-line paraphrase should be avoided. Cover… ------ 1 Purpose 2 When and under what conditions it's invoked 3 Inputs, preconditions and invariants 4 The algorithm, in meaningful groups 5 Important branches 6 Borrowed versus owned state 7 Result or emission, plus errors and partiality 8 Downstream consumers 9 Rationale (why it's built this way) 10 The exact source reference The metadata index is the scaffold, not an assertion that this prose is already complete.

title: Module dependency explorer
summary: 12 · Module dependency explorer In one sentence: A dependency says one part of the code refers to another. It says nothing about what happened in a specific C execution. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Module A named group of Rust d
text: 12 · Module dependency explorer In one sentence: A dependency says one part of the code refers to another. It says nothing about what happened in a specific C execution. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Module A named group of Rust definitions, often backed by one source file or directory. Dependency A source-level reference, such as using another module's type. Some dependencies are about data, not function calls. Example. The parser depends on the shared models definitions because it reads the trace format the engine wrote. That doesn't give the parser any control over a running debugger. How to read the maps Treat these as subsystem-level dependency and data-flow relationships. A module reference is not necessarily an executed call, because several boundaries aren't function calls at all: - external processes (GCC, GDB, Valgrind), - serialization (writing and reading JSON), and - optional metadata (Clang). When you need a specific call path, select a real function in the call-flow explorer(call-flow.html) and check its direct evidence. Engine module groups {{diagram:engine-subsystems}} Point Explanation ------ Entry/orchestration layer Owns the session result. Shared models Used by the recorder, diagnostics and parser. That doesn't make them peer processes. C wrapper ↔ Rust The C wrapper writes a file that Rust reads later. There is no Rust-to-C function call in the tracing loop. Parser module groups {{diagram:parser-subsystems}} Layer Role ------ Parsing Owns the canonical trace Indexes Own positions (not copies of records) Raw and validated views Borrow the trace Name clash: src/trace_parser/semantic.rs is Stage 1 qualification. Don't confuse it with src/semantic/, the excluded Stage 2 implementation. Sources and limits {{diagram:module-dependencies}} The file inventory(files.html) shows each file's outbound module references, labeled as static references. They are not certified function calls. This alone… …does not prove ------ A shared data type A particular function invocation An imported module A particular function invocation Graph edges carry distinct classifications and source evidence instead.

title: Interactive call-flow explorer
summary: 13 · Interactive call-flow explorer In one sentence: An interactive map of reviewed paths through the Stage 1 code. The arrow labels say what kind of relationship each arrow shows. Arrow types Label Meaning ------ Direct A checked
text: 13 · Interactive call-flow explorer In one sentence: An interactive map of reviewed paths through the Stage 1 code. The arrow labels say what kind of relationship each arrow shows. Arrow types Label Meaning ------ Direct A checked call expression in source: one function explicitly calls another. Callback dispatch A call routed through a callback rather than named directly. Subprocess communication Talking to an external process (GCC, GDB). Data handoff Data passed from one part to another, such as a file or struct. Conceptual Two parts belong to the same explanation; no runtime function call is claimed. Dashed / candidate A possible link. It is not an invocation. These types stay visually and textually distinct on the graph. Example. Select the path from trace_program to GDB capture. Open each source link to verify exactly where a function is called, and use the other arrow types for tool or data boundaries. An arrow between source functions does not mean that route ran in every recorded trace. What the graph covers It follows selected verified Stage 1 production relationships: CLI → trace → JSON loading → validation → consumer queries Two nodes are explicitly labeled external tools (GCC and GDB). They stand for process boundaries and are not made-up Rust functions. The graph is deliberately selective. If a function is missing, check the complete function index(functions.html). Selecting a node shows its source, purpose, incoming and outgoing edges, each with its classification and supporting references. Exploring - Filter by subsystem, or search by function or path. - Select a node to expand its neighborhood. - Walk a multi-module path by choosing adjacent nodes. Interactive graph {{explorer}} Guided execution paths The Guided path selector offers six source-verified tours: Tour ------ 1 CLI → export 2 GDB stop → checkpoint 3 Allocator wrapper → heap lifetime 4 DWARF extraction → type registry 5 JSON input → checkpoint summary 6 Deep validation → semantic confidence Previous and Next move one real graph node at a time, and each step names the relationship and its source location. Choose Free exploration to return to the full neighborhood view. Where the data comes from - Graph entries live in assets/call-flow.js with stable IDs and source references. - A path:line is copyable. Local source files open without assuming your browser supports line anchors. - No Stage 2 symbol is included. - This graph is a guided subset, not a complete dynamic call graph. The DOC-2/DOC-3 chapters give deeper explanations; future reviewed edges can be added without changing the frontend.

title: Compilation & diagnostics
summary: 14 · Compilation and compiler diagnostics In one sentence: Before a debugger can inspect C, GCC has to build a real program. If that fails, the trace records the failure and does not pretend a run happened. Key terms Term Meaning
text: 14 · Compilation and compiler diagnostics In one sentence: Before a debugger can inspect C, GCC has to build a real program. If that fails, the trace records the failure and does not pretend a run happened. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Debug build An executable with source-to-machine debug information and the project's allocation wrapper linked in. Sanitizer build A separate executable with compiler-added memory checks. It can fail or be skipped independently of the debug build. Example. For return missing_symbol;, GCC reports a compiler error. The trace keeps that error and has zero GDB snapshots, rather than inventing a run that never started. A successful sanitizer build also doesn't mean its separate execution ran or found no errors. Level 1 · Intuition Visual C needs a real executable with debug information, not a guess from reading C text. It runs GCC on your sources and keeps warnings and errors as structured diagnostics. If compilation fails, the trace says so and does not pretend the debugger ran. The same project can also produce a separate sanitizer build for a later diagnostic run. {{diagram:compilation}} Level 2 · Build lifecycle What describes the request Config Holds ------ BuildConfig The C files and compiler options (include directories, extra flags) TraceConfig Everything in BuildConfig, plus the program's own arguments, output path, time and byte limits, and optional tools The two builds Debug variant Sanitizer variant --------- Built by compiler::compile_project The same function (a different build) Includes the allocator wrapper (c_runtime/alloc_tracker.c)? Yes No How allocations are logged Linker switches -Wl,--wrap=malloc (and similar for calloc, realloc, free) send calls through a small logging function before the real allocator Not wrapped Compiler checks Debug info ASan/UBSan (AddressSanitizer for memory errors, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer for undefined C behavior) Used for The primary GDB run A later, separate diagnostic run Other build details: - The engine detects which compiler-diagnostic format GCC supports, and saves each error with a file, line, kind and message. - Time and output bounds apply while GCC runs. - User-supplied flags can change what the compiler emits, so keep them in mind when comparing runs. What happens if the build fails Situation Result ------ GCC rejects the C source compiled_successfully=false, execution_status=compile_failed; the compiler's explanation is kept; later debugger stages are marked skipped; snapshots= (there was no program to pause) GCC fails to start, or a deadline expires A different kind of failure from GCC rejecting your source Debug build succeeds The engine can read DWARF type information and start GDB Sanitizer executable builds Says nothing about whether its separate run found, or ruled out, a crash Level 3 · Files, signatures and example File Provides ------ src/config.rs::{BuildConfig, TraceConfig, SanitizerTrigger} The request src/compiler.rs::{CompileOptions, compile_project, detect_diagnostics_format} Both build variants and error formats src/trace.rs::trace_program_inner Assigns stage_results.compiler; short-circuits on failed compilation src/models.rs::{CompilerDiagnostic, StageResults, StageResult} Structured outcomes src/supervisor.rs Subprocess groups and session deadlines c // Source fixture: fixtures/c/phase8b_defined.c (abridged) int oracle_global = 41; static int checkpoint(struct Packet packet, int alias, int heap, int sum) { volatile int value = packet-items1 + alias + heap2 + sum + oracle_global; return value; } sh cargo build --release target/release/c-trace-engine fixtures/c/phase8b_defined.c \ --trace-mode dual --max-steps 350 --timeout 50 --no-pretty \ --sanitizer-trigger never --output /tmp/visual-c-defined.json A real failure case. From the final integrated audit(../stage1-final-audit.md): a deliberately invalid return missing_symbol; produced an engine JSON trace with execution_status="compile_failed", one compiler diagnostic, and zero snapshots and events. For safe output inspection see practical usage(usage.htmllevel-2-run-a-recording); for independent analysis stages see diagnostics(engine-diagnostics.html). Note: Tool availability is checked before compilation. GCC and GDB are required. A missing Valgrind or addr2line is reported and qualified, not treated as a successful zero-error analysis. No part of this pipeline is a sandbox for hostile C.

title: GDB/MI and checkpoints
summary: 15 · GDB/MI execution and checkpoints In one sentence: A debugger pause is a photograph, not a video of everything between two pauses. The engine must also tell a command reply apart from a real new stop. Key terms Term Meaning --
text: 15 · GDB/MI execution and checkpoints In one sentence: A debugger pause is a photograph, not a video of everything between two pauses. The engine must also tell a command reply apart from a real new stop. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Program counter (PC) The machine address of the instruction GDB is about to execute at a stop. It is not automatically an instruction that already ran. MI acknowledgement GDB saying it accepted a command (^running). A separate stopped message says the program actually stopped later. Inferior The program GDB is controlling. Example. At one stop, GDB reads sum=10. That value belongs to that stop. If an instruction step never reports another stop, the engine can't claim the attempted instruction completed. Three different numbers: a stop counter, a snapshot's vector index and an attempted-instruction position are separate. Never swap them. Level 1 · Intuition A stopped program is observable; code running between stops is not automatically known. The GDB/MI2 driver sends commands, waits for each response and for the asynchronous stops, and inspects bounded source state. - At a stop, the PC names the next instruction. - An instruction attempt is recorded from that before address, plus a next address only when observed. - Source checkpoints are selected stops, not a reconstruction of every intermediate state. {{diagram:checkpoint}} Level 2 · Command/response lifecycle What the engine does at a chosen pause 1. GDB starts the debug program and pauses it. 2. The engine notes the function and source line. 3. It reads available variables and heap bytes, within the configured budgets. 4. It collects new allocator log lines. 5. It assigns the stop a stop_id that increases as stops are observed. Stepping one instruction In dual source-and-instruction mode, the engine can send -exec-step-instruction. engine ──► -exec-step-instruction GDB ──► ^running ← only means "I started the step" GDB ──► stopped ← NOW we know where execution stopped An InstructionEvent stores the address before the attempted step, its event number and context, and a next address only when observed. Situation How it's handled ------ The stop never arrives Reported differently from the whole session running out of time A command reply is missing Late text is not handed to a different command Breakpoint hit Gives the engine a stop, but that alone doesn't prove the attempted instruction finished Stepping skips a library interval A TraceGap(model.htmlevents-gaps-and-checkpoints) marks what was not recorded, instead of inventing a number of missing instructions How a step is classified A step can be recorded as completed, faulted, interrupted or unknown. What GDB does not cover - The engine may set bounded breakpoints to catch some callbacks, but a function appearing in source is not evidence it was called. - GDB pauses its selected debugging session. Outside processes and unfollowed fork children are not guaranteed snapshots. - Observing one thread does not give a complete timeline of all threads. Worked example: a stop, then a parser query At source line 15 of fixtures/c/phase8b_defined.c, the audited live capture recorded: Item Value ------ Variable integer sum Displayed value "10" Raw bytes "0a000000" (Linux little-endian) Independent check Native GDB, in a separate run, printed sum=10 A later TraceStore can fetch that snapshot by its vector index, and checkpoint_summary() can page its variables. Neither the stop ID nor the value of instruction_position should be used as that vector index. See the API walkthrough(usage.htmlcheckpoints-and-paging). Level 3 · Source and invariants File Owns ------ src/gdb_mi.rs MI command tokens, async records, stop backlog, frame parsing, selected-thread tracking, memory reads src/mi_parser.rs MI syntax parsing src/trace.rs The stop loop and push_snapshot src/recorder.rs::{checkpoint, event, gap, event_outcome} Appends bounded canonical records and journal lines src/models.rs::{SnapshotObservation, InstructionEvent, TraceGap} The serializable identities src/trace_parser/indexes.rs::OrderingFacts Enables binary search only when order is verified json {"step_index":0,"observation":{"stop_id":1,"instruction_position":0,"heap_event_count":0}} This JSON is illustrative and deliberately partial. A real ExecutionSnapshot has required file, function, call stack and variable fields. In it: Field What it is ------ stop_id=1 A debugger stop counter step_index=0 A snapshot vector index instruction_position=0 A count of attempts before this stop See schema identity domains(schema.htmlidentity-domains). Warning: Recording a checkpoint_id on an instruction event associates it with the most recent checkpoint. It is not a claim that the instruction happened precisely at that checkpoint stop, or that a source-line AST expression executed.

title: Frames, variables & memory
summary: 16 · Stack frames, variables and raw memory In one sentence: A variable can have a displayed value, an address and captured raw bytes. They are related observations that answer different questions. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Fr
text: 16 · Stack frames, variables and raw memory In one sentence: A variable can have a displayed value, an address and captured raw bytes. They are related observations that answer different questions. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Frame activation One particular call of a function. Two recursive calls have two activations even if both have a local named n. Captured prefix The bytes actually read from the start of an object. A missing tail has not been filled with zeros. Example. For int p, address is where the variable p itself lives; points_to is the address stored inside it. Reading p successfully doesn't prove the memory at its target is alive or initialized. The debugger can also read bytes from an uninitialized object. Being readable is not an initialization test. Level 1 · Intuition A displayed debugger value is an observation made at one stopped moment, not proof of C-language initialization. Visual C records: - where a variable lived, - what GDB could display, - whether bytes were actually read, and - which limits prevented a fuller read. Each function call creates a new frame activation, so two locals named n in different recursive calls are not the same variable. {{diagram:stack}} Level 2 · At a stopped checkpoint Where things live in a snapshot An ExecutionSnapshot is one saved pause. Part of the snapshot Holds ------ variables Variables of the currently selected function call, called frame 0 caller_frames (If configured) bounded information about the functions that called it snapshot.observation.globals Globals and file-static variables call_stack Frames with their GDB levels The position of an item inside caller_frames is a different index from a GDB level. Don't swap them. Each observed call has an activation ID, so recurse(3).value and recurse(2).value are never merged just because both locals are named value. - GDB's Python support can help find exact lexical blocks and read a shadowed variable. - If those details are unavailable, the engine labels the weaker fallback rather than pretending it has the same identity confidence. - A variable being in scope does not prove its initializer has run. The two addresses of a pointer For int p: Field Meaning ------ VariableInfo.address Where the pointer variable p itself is stored points_to The address value inside p address_match_allocation_id=7 A possible numeric match, if the target lies in heap block 7. It does not say p originally came from block 7. Addresses may be reused. Separate memory questions, separate fields Field Answers ------ read_status What GDB's printed value looked like bytes_status Whether the raw byte read succeeded memory_evidence How many bytes were requested and how many captured initialization_status Whether it was initialized. Separate, and often unknown If only the first four of eight bytes were captured, raw_bytes_hex contains that four-byte prefix. The other four have not been read or zero-filled. A requested per-instruction memory region belongs only to its actual instruction stop. Bytes saved at an older checkpoint are historical elsewhere. Worked call c // Illustrative C; see fixtures/c/recursive.c for the real tested fixture. int recurse(int value) { if (value == 0) return 1; return value recurse(value - 1); } When recurse(3) calls recurse(2), the second frame is a distinct activation. - The audited engine trace with limits.max_caller_frames=3 captured 45 caller-frame entries across 26 snapshots. That is not an unlimited call history. - Each checkpoint is a historical observation: later returns or frees must not change earlier captures. - The TP-7 frame activation(parser-consumer.htmllevel-3-real-signatures-and-bounded-traversal) query resolves only within one retained snapshot. Level 3 · Where to look File Role ------ src/gdb_mi.rs Extracts StackFrameInfo, RawVariable and bounded GDB reads src/trace.rs::push_snapshot Collects checkpoint state, heap blocks and caller frames src/memory.rs Enriches byte and target observations src/recorder.rs::set_validity Keeps display status and byte status distinct src/dwarf.rs::associate Correlates unique declarations without replacing GDB values src/models.rs::{ExecutionSnapshot, SnapshotObservation, VariableInfo, MemoryEvidence, FrameVariables, ScopeStatus, DataValidity} The schema src/trace_parser/semantic.rs::MemoryEvidenceView Qualifies captured byte ranges without decoding C semantics json {"name":"sum","value":"10","raw_bytes_hex":"0a000000","read_status":"valid","bytes_status":"valid"} This is an abridged excerpt of the audited phase8b_defined.c:15 variable, not a stand-alone VariableInfo document. Four readable bytes show a captured representation of 10, not proof of prior initialization. See the data model(model.htmlvariables-bytes-and-heap) and confidence(parser-semantic.html). Note: Caller capture defaults to max_caller_frames=0. A missing caller vector is not evidence the program had no caller. Per-snapshot and per-variable read budgets may truncate capture without invalidating the other observations.

title: DWARF, Clang & fusion
summary: 17 · DWARF, Clang AST and evidence fusion In one sentence: Type information comes from the built program and optional syntax information from the source. Neither replaces reading runtime memory. Key terms Term Meaning ------ DWARF
text: 17 · DWARF, Clang AST and evidence fusion In one sentence: Type information comes from the built program and optional syntax information from the source. Neither replaces reading runtime memory. Key terms Term Meaning ------ DWARF Compiler-written debug info describing compiled types, declarations and source locations. AST Clang's tree of written C syntax. It can show a call appears in the source without showing the program took that branch. Fusion One cautious pass that links existing records from different providers. It never supplies new values or invents writes. Example. Three tools answer three different questions: Tool Question it answers ------ DWARF Where is struct Pair.y located inside the compiled struct? GDB What bytes were there at this stop? Clang Is there a written malloc call in the source? A same-line source match is only a candidate, especially if macros or several calls share that line. Level 1 · Intuition Static metadata helps explain what a stopped value might be: DWARF identifies the compiler's types and declarations, and optional Clang AST identifies syntax and source spans. GDB supplies the dynamic runtime values. None of the static sources proves a C expression executed. {{diagram:metadata}} Level 2 · The three evidence streams Stream 1: DWARF Step What happens ------ dwarf::extract_excluding Reads debug info from the program GCC actually built, leaves out the injected allocator logger, and saves bounded lists of compiled types and declarations in TypeRegistry dwarf::associate (later) Links a stopped GDB variable to a type or declaration only when it finds a unique match; keeps the observed size and address exactly as GDB reported them Stream 2: Clang AST (optional, --clang-ast) - Clang separately reads the C source into SourceMetadataRegistry. - A missing Clang tool or partly parsed source is marked missing or partial, not mistaken for an empty program. - GCC and Clang can use different compilation settings, so a link between their descriptions isn't always justified. Stream 3: Fusion After the engine finishes capturing runtime and reconstructing the heap, evidence::fuse makes one cautious linking pass: File Handles ------ declarations.rs Compiled declarations and members source_links.rs Links to observed variables heap.rs Marks possible source locations for allocator calls validation.rs Removes links that can't be supported The summary counts links kept and rejected. Fusion does Fusion does not ------ Link existing records, cautiously Ask GDB for new values Count kept and rejected links Copy the type registry for every pause Turn a possible source call into an executed call The parser later stores positions for these metadata IDs instead of cloning their records. Worked ambiguity Two heap-call expressions on one source line, or a macro expanding to one, can share a line with a recorded allocation event. The relationship can be a candidate or ambiguous. A same-line match is never a dynamic expression-to-event identity. So TP-6 source_expression(id).execution_confidence stays Unavailable even when heap_call_candidates exist. This matters when writing future Stage 2 explanations(handoff.htmllevel-2-the-freeze-contract). Level 3 · Files and API File / function Role ------ src/dwarf.rs::{TypeRegistry, extract_excluding, associate} Reads ELF/DWARF, matches unique declarations, reports missing or ambiguous data src/clang_ast.rs::{SourceMetadataRegistry, analyze, correlate_heap_calls} Produces optional static syntax src/evidence/mod.rs::fuse and src/evidence/{declarations,source_links,heap,validation}.rs Bounded reconciliation src/models.rs::EvidenceFusionSummary Serializes the counts TraceStore::type_entry(id), dwarf_declaration(id), source_declaration(id), source_expression(id) Return borrowed, indexed metadata ValidatedSemanticView::source_expression(id) Adds confidence plus indexed candidate/ambiguity event positions rust // Real TP-6 API; expression IDs belong to this trace, not to other runs. let expression = validated.source_expression(expression_id); let syntax = expression.expression; // Option<&SourceExpression let execution = expression.execution_confidence; // Unavailable on sound traces for candidate in expression.call_sites() { let _ = (candidate.event_position, candidate.event); } The snippet assumes validated and expression_id are already defined. Run the complete parser walkthrough(usage.htmllevel-3-load-and-validate) first. Signatures are in the public API reference(api.htmllevel-3-signatures-and-contracts). Warning: "source line observed" is not "specific AST expression executed." Never use an AST call candidate to grant pointer provenance or to allocate a new runtime lifetime.

title: Allocation lifetimes
summary: 18 · Allocation events, lifetimes and realloc In one sentence: Think of allocations as lifetimes, not addresses. A freed address can be handed out again to a brand-new block. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Wrapper A small function
text: 18 · Allocation events, lifetimes and realloc In one sentence: Think of allocations as lifetimes, not addresses. A freed address can be handed out again to a brand-new block. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Wrapper A small function inserted before a linked call to malloc, calloc, realloc or free. It logs the call and passes it on to the real allocator. Lifetime ID A number given to a tracked allocation's period of existence. Two blocks can share an address without sharing this ID. A lifetime, step by step malloc(…) → ID 1 created at address A free(A) → ID 1 ends malloc(…) → ID 2 created at address A again ← same address, different lifetime A successful in-place realloc also starts a new lifetime ID in this engine, even though it keeps address A. Limit: The logger cannot promise to see allocators that run entirely inside unwrapped shared libraries. Level 1 · Intuition The same numeric address can host many unrelated allocations over time. Stage 1: - gives each intercepted allocation a lifetime ID, - records the events that affect it, and - keeps snapshots immutable (later events never rewrite earlier captures). A current pointer's address can fall inside a block's range without proving which lifetime produced the pointer. realloc can retire one lifetime and create a linked successor. A failed realloc must not retire the original. {{diagram:heap}} Level 2 · From logged events to reconstructed lifetimes On the C side (c_runtime/alloc_tracker.c) 1. --wrap=malloc redirects linked malloc calls through a wrapper. The wrapper calls the real malloc once and returns its actual result. Other wrappers handle calloc, realloc and free. 2. A fixed-size C table remembers each tracked address, allocation ID and size. 3. Each event is written to a dedicated file with its PID and an increasing number for that process. 4. A guard stops the logger from recursively logging its own allocator work. On the Rust side 1. At each debugger pause, EventTailer reads the complete new lines. 2. HeapTimeline::ingest builds block lifetimes from them, marking missing, duplicated or out-of-order lines instead of assuming a perfect history. 3. The engine reads the event file before taking the stopped-state snapshot. 4. It may look up a recorded caller instruction address in the live process's maps, but an unresolved source location stays unresolved. How realloc is handled Case What the recorder does ------ Successful, block moves New, linked lifetime ID Successful, block stays at the same address New, linked lifetime ID (same treatment) Failed realloc The old block stays alive realloc(ptr, 0) in the observed glibc environment May free the old block and return NULL. The logged terminal event uses the old ID, with no new address or size, so it is not a link to a new block The parser checks recorded events and lifetime boundaries before it says two IDs are connected. Equal addresses alone can't prove that. See realloc validation(parser-validation.htmlrealloc-link-verification). What each heap record means Evidence Meaning Caution --------- HeapEvent Wrapper event in ingestion order: PID, sequence, IDs, kind, optional address ID 0 is untracked; internal library allocators may be invisible HeapBlockInfo Final or historical state, with optional realloc predecessor Freed block bytes are historical; check observed_at_stop AllocationLifetime PID, allocation sequence, optional free sequence Complete observed-PID history is not a fork census HeapHistoryCoverage Gaps, transport, ACK, caps, process scope complete=true has a specific observed-PID scope Level 3 · C/Rust boundary and example c // Source: fixtures/c/realloc_move.c (excerpt) char p = malloc(32); char guard = malloc(32); char next = realloc(p, 1024 1024); if (!next) { free(p); free(guard); return 1; } free(next); For a successful move, the raw event carries old_allocation_id, a new allocation_id and the recorded PID/sequence. The old lifetime ends at that event's sequence. In the final parser, heap(new_id).realloc_confidence is Definite only when all four hold: 1. a matching creation event exists, 2. the predecessor's creation is recorded, 3. same-PID lifetime boundaries are compatible, and 4. the observed history is complete and verified. Partial or legacy evidence stays candidate or unavailable. src/trace_parser/validation.rs::realloc_link performs the shared relationship checks, and structural contradictions and cycles can never become definite. Layer Where to look ------ C __wrap_malloc, __wrap_calloc, __wrap_realloc, __wrap_free, cte_emit_locked, cte_after_fork_child in c_runtime/alloc_tracker.c Rust src/allocation_tracker.rs::{parse_event_line, EventTailer, HeapTimeline::ingest, verify_event_status}; src/trace.rs backfills snapshots and builds final state Parser TraceStore::heap_events_for_allocation(id) uses a position index; ValidatedSemanticView::heap(id) qualifies identity and realloc separately. See schema fields(schema.htmlheap-records) Warning: The wrapper does not intercept allocator calls made entirely inside unwrapped shared libraries. The transport's terminal ACK verifies only observed PIDs plus the followed inferior. No absolute heap completeness or descendant coverage is promised.

title: Valgrind & sanitizers
summary: 19 · Independent diagnostics · Valgrind and sanitizers In one sentence: Memory-error tools add valuable clues, but they run separately from the main GDB observation, so their findings belong to their own runs. Key terms Term Meani
text: 19 · Independent diagnostics · Valgrind and sanitizers In one sentence: Memory-error tools add valuable clues, but they run separately from the main GDB observation, so their findings belong to their own runs. Key terms Term Meaning ------ Valgrind Runs the program under memory checking and reports leaks or invalid accesses. Generally slower. Sanitizer Compiler-inserted checks in a separately built program, such as AddressSanitizer for memory misuse. Example. A Valgrind leak at line 52 may point you at useful source code. It cannot identify "allocation 17" from the debugger's run just because that run also visited line 52. Each analysis records its own status. A skipped or failed analysis is not the same as "checked, no errors found." Level 1 · Intuition GDB shows what happened in the primary traced run. Valgrind and sanitizer runs can detect memory problems the primary trace doesn't prove, but they execute the program again. - A similar address or source line across executions is not the same allocation. - A diagnostic belongs to its own run. - Missing or truncated output is not a clean bill of health. {{diagram:metadata}} Level 2 · Stages and uncertainty Valgrind Point Detail ------ How it runs Starts another execution and writes an XML report What the engine reads Complete error entries, leak details and summary numbers Truncated output recover_errors keeps the <error entries that were fully written, and marks the whole report incomplete Missing leak total Means "we don't know the total," not zero (even if an older default field contains 0) The allocation wrapper Does not actively track blocks in the Valgrind run, because its own table could make leaks look reachable and hide the problem Sanitizer It is compiled into a different executable. The sanitizer_trigger setting chooses when it runs: Setting Runs the sanitizer… ------ never Never after a crash Only if the primary run crashed after a crash or Valgrind error Default always Always The trace records whether the stage was skipped, timed out, failed or completed. Situation How it's treated ------ An ASan report and a primary GDB crash have a supported source-location match May be shown together as related clues No such support The sanitizer finding stays independent Nonzero exit, no usable diagnostic Inconclusive, not proof of a memory bug A deadline arrives May stop optional checks Valgrind fails Does not change the status of the program's primary run Worked crash: a useful prefix, separate completeness c // Source: fixtures/c/phase8r3_crash.c int observed_global = 123; int main(void) { (volatile int )0 = observed_global; return 0; } In a fresh audited run, this produced: Result Value ------ execution_status "crashed" Crash report SIGSEGV Snapshots 3 Retained instruction attempts 5 coverage.complete_for_scope true (for the observed user-code interval) heap_history.complete false (the allocation tracker got no normal terminal ACK) These are different dimensions. Neither the crash nor the heap partiality erases the captured stops, and a complete user-code scope does not make heap history complete. With a forced sanitizer pass, the separately run sanitizer also produced a diagnostic. Don't infer unrecorded writes or a complete process-tree history from the retained prefix. Source site is not identity - src/valgrind.rs::correlate_with_allocations is a legacy-name helper that now ignores supplied primary allocation IDs. - It may produce ID-free same-absolute-file/line candidates, but never an exact cross-run allocation link. - Imported legacy related_allocation_ids can remain in raw reports, yet TP-6 valgrind_error(index).primary_allocation_id is always None. See confidence contracts(parser-semantic.htmlindependent-diagnostics). Level 3 · Models and real failure path File / item Role ------ src/valgrind.rs::{parse_valgrind_xml, recover_errors, correlate_with_allocations} Valgrind parsing and recovery src/sanitizer.rs::{parse_sanitizer_output, matches_crash} Sanitizer parsing and crash matching src/trace.rs Schedules passes and records stage_results src/models.rs::{ValgrindReport, ValgrindError, SanitizerReport, CrashReport, StageResult} Holds outputs ValidatedSemanticView::diagnostics() Borrows the session reports valgrind_error(index) A trace-local reference to an independent diagnostic rust let diagnostics = validated.diagnostics(); if let Some(report) = diagnostics.valgrind { for index in 0..report.detailed_errors.len() { let item = validated.valgrind_error(index)?; assert!(item.primary_allocation_id.is_none()); } } The code assumes a previously defined validated view; see the runnable usage example(usage.htmllevel-3-load-and-validate). In the final Stage 1 audit, a fresh Valgrind fixture produced one native diagnostic and zero primary allocation links. The crash and forced-sanitizer samples each kept only the reports actually observed. A missing report is never a negative diagnosis. Warning: A primary-run allocation ID found in an imported Valgrind raw field is not an authorized Stage 2 identity join. Never use matching source, address, PID or name across executions as a substitute for same-execution event evidence.
