title: Subsystem walkthroughs
summary: 36 · Engine subsystem walkthroughs In one sentence: Each section follows one actual route through several engine files. Read it as a story of what data changes hands. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Call path The sequence of c
text: 36 · Engine subsystem walkthroughs In one sentence: Each section follows one actual route through several engine files. Read it as a story of what data changes hands. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Call path The sequence of checked functions and tool boundaries used in a particular explanation. Intermediate data A record made between input and output, such as a GDB stop or a wrapper event line. Example. For an allocation story, follow a C malloc call to the wrapper's file, then the Rust reader, then the saved heap event. At each step ask what might have been missed. What not to assume: An example route does not assert that optional stages ran in every execution or that a source candidate proves a runtime call. The big picture These are six illustrative source-guided sequences, not a transcript of one executed trace. A C statement in an example is not proof that it ran: only a recorded stop, allocation event, or diagnostic from its own execution supports the corresponding claim. The Stage 1 final integrated audit(../stage1-final-audit.md) is historical evidence, not a rerun for this page; its fixture counts and outcomes must not be read as measurements of a new invocation. Each walkthrough stops at an engine subsystem boundary rather than following one program end to end. A. Compiling a C project into two different artifacts Example and transition fixtures/c/phase8b_defined.c:19-27 contains int heap = malloc(3 sizeof(int)); followed by a checked realloc. This source illustrates a build input, not a claim that either call executed. src/main.rs:24-34 converts CLI options to TraceConfig and calls trace::trace_program; src/trace.rs:132-165 validates limits and establishes the overall supervisor::scope deadline. trace_program_inner checks inspection expressions, probes required GCC/GDB and optional Valgrind/addr2line, creates a session directory, then writes the embedded c_runtime/alloc_tracker.c through allocation_tracker::write_runtime_source (src/trace.rs:167-235, src/allocation_tracker.rs:30-37). The resulting tracker_source is a real additional translation unit, not a source rewrite of the user's C. compiler::compile_project (src/compiler.rs:529-581) detects the accepted diagnostics format and calls compile for the debug variant first. build_argv puts -g -O0 -fno-omit-frame-pointer and the four linker --wrap flags before user flags, then sources, objects and link options (src/compiler.rs:392-451); user flags can override defaults. Only after debug success does compile_project attempt the separate unwrapped sanitized binary, trying address,undefined, then address, then undefined. Its result is a pair of CompilationOutput records: success, exit_code, binary path, diagnostics, raw stderr, and selected diagnostics format (src/compiler.rs:75-97,454-527). The debug artifact is the one GDB later executes; building an ASan artifact does not run it. detect_diagnostics_format probes JSON, SARIF-to-stderr, then text (src/compiler.rs:130-158); compile normalizes compiler diagnostics, falling back to text_diagnostics for unparseable output/linker errors (src/compiler.rs:232-258,317-390,493-526). supervisor::output enforces a deadline and bounded subprocess output (src/supervisor.rs:226-260). If invocation/deadline fails, trace_program_inner returns a partial trace with compiler stage failed/timed out and subsequent stages skipped (src/trace.rs:238-289). If GCC instead returns a failed debug build, compiled_successfully=false, compile_errors is populated, ExecutionStatus::CompileFailed is recorded and GDB is not started (src/trace.rs:291-349). A failed optional sanitized build keeps a successful debug build and notes degraded diagnostics (src/compiler.rs:552-580, src/trace.rs:392-414). The CLI exports a returned compile-failure trace but exits 2; an operational Err exits 1 (src/main.rs:34-78). text CLI - trace_program_inner: TraceConfig + session deadline trace_program_inner - write_runtime_source: embedded tracker - session/alloc_tracker.c trace_program_inner - compile_project - compile: debug GCC argv + wrapper TU compile_project - compile: optional unwrapped sanitizer variant(s) compile_project - trace_program_inner: (debug CompilationOutput, asan CompilationOutput) trace_program_inner - trace: compiler StageResult; failed debug build - skip GDB Source details: entry(engine-entry-deep.html), compiler(engine-compiler-deep.html), supervision(engine-supervision-deep.html), export(engine-export-deep.html). B. Turning a GDB stop into a source checkpoint Example and transition fixtures/c/phase8b_defined.c:13-16 has a non-inlined checkpoint function reading a packet, alias, heap element and global. Those expressions describe possible observations; a line number alone cannot establish values or execution. After compilation, trace_program_inner creates UserCodeClassifier, EventFileReader and HeapTimeline, and passes optional dwarf::ObservationTypes to run_gdb_phase (src/trace.rs:416-439). GdbSession::launch starts gdb --nx --quiet --interpreter=mi2, configures all-stop mode, PTY output, arguments and the allocator event-file environment (src/trace.rs:1171-1189, src/gdb_mi.rs:385-511). insert_breakpoint("main"), install_user_entries and run start observed stops; a missing main breakpoint allows execution to completion without intermediate stepping snapshots (src/trace.rs:1226-1249). MI text is parsed by mi_parser::parse_line; gdb_mi::route_record delivers tokened ^ results to the pending command and asynchronous stopped records separately, while GdbSession::wait_stopped returns a StoppedInfo with frame/reason/thread information (src/mi_parser.rs:559-636, src/gdb_mi.rs:623-671,2302-2444). At each stop, run_gdb_phase first ingests complete allocator lines, then classifies exit/signal, then checks whether the frame belongs to user code (src/trace.rs:1371-1568). In dual mode, a source checkpoint is created on a changed (file,line,func) or breakpoint hit; repeated same-source instruction stops can still produce instruction events without another snapshot. Source-only mode uses exec_step, whereas dual mode uses exec_instruction; non-user frames are normally finished or continued rather than traced as user instructions (src/trace.rs:1562-1568,1720-1751,1799-1929). For an eligible checkpoint, gdb_mi::capture_state produces CapturedState with frames, bounded frame-zero variables, optionally caller-frame variables, errors and memory used (src/gdb_mi.rs:1738-1749,1840-1964,2177-2227). recorder::capture_variable_memory attempts actual stopped-inferior byte reads under object/checkpoint budgets, records partial/unreadable status, and leaves initialization_status="unknown" (src/recorder.rs:45-185). push_snapshot spends only the remaining snapshot budget on currently alive observed heap blocks and creates ExecutionSnapshot; capture_requested_globals, memory::enrich_snapshot, finalize_memory_coverage, and Recorder::checkpoint add qualified globals/pointer evidence, memory errors and the checkpoint journal record (src/trace.rs:1609-1677,2179-2304,2356-2476, src/recorder.rs:259-265). SnapshotObservation carries stop_id, instruction position, PID, thread, origin and heap-event count, not an exact allocation-call timestamp. If frame mapping, lexical metadata, reads, budgets, or GDB commands fail, partial captures and errors are retained; capture_or_empty preserves an otherwise lost stop (src/trace.rs:2162-2176). text GDB --MI2 - route_record - wait_stopped: tokened result + async StoppedInfo run_gdb_phase - EventFileReader/HeapTimeline: ingest available complete lines run_gdb_phase - capture_state: bounded frames/variables/bytes at this stop run_gdb_phase - push_snapshot: remaining-budget live heap - ExecutionSnapshot run_gdb_phase - globals/enrich_snapshot/finalize_memory_coverage run_gdb_phase - Recorder::checkpoint: stop-indexed checkpoint (or explicit cap) Source details: GDB control(engine-gdb-deep.html), MI protocol(engine-mi-deep.html), recorder(engine-recorder-deep.html), stack capture(engine-stack-deep.html), heap(engine-heap-deep.html). C. From a wrapped malloc to a qualified heap observation Example and transition fixtures/c/pointer_demo.c:7-19 includes int heap = malloc(4 sizeof(int));, writes elements and later frees the block. Illustrative conditional sequence: if that call executes successfully under the wrapped debug binary, __wrap_malloc calls the real allocator exactly once, assigns a process-local ID, emits pid seq malloc id addr size old_id old_addr caller status to the dedicated append-only event file, and inserts the returned address in its fixed table (c_runtime/alloc_tracker.c:343-361,265-287). It does not print allocator events to program stdout. --wrap covers references from linked objects, not allocations internal to shared libraries (c_runtime/alloc_tracker.c:41-47). A failed allocation emits failed and no live block; a zero-sized request may return either NULL or a non-NULL block, so its outcome must come from the event, not the syntax. EventFileReader::read_new tails at most a 1 MiB segment per stop, buffers an unfinished line, and parse_event_line turns a complete line into RawEvent (src/allocation_tracker.rs:65-159,262-399). HeapTimeline::ingest checks (pid, seq), adds a successful malloc as BlockState indexed by (pid,id) and (pid,address), updates live-byte usage, then appends HeapEvent::Allocated (src/allocation_tracker.rs:406-485,521-605,768-855). A sequence gap, duplicate, malformed transport or retention cap downgrades history; it must not manufacture a live block from later events (src/allocation_tracker.rs:501-567). Recorder::allocations journals newly ingested events with the stop at which they were noticed, not the precise execution stop of the call (src/recorder.rs:267-285). At a later observed checkpoint, push_snapshot calls alive_blocks(pid), reads live memory via capture_variable_memory, and creates HeapBlockInfo with ID/address/extent and read evidence; a block not observed at a stop has no captured bytes for that stop (src/trace.rs:2179-2277, src/allocation_tracker.rs:861-873). memory::enrich_snapshot can annotate pointer address candidates but address equality alone cannot prove pointer origin (src/trace.rs:1667-1672). After the GDB phase, optional resolve_caller_locations and apply_caller_locations map the wrapper's raw return PC minus the executable bias and one instruction byte back to a file/line; an unresolved address remains a raw PC (src/trace.rs:590-637, src/allocation_tracker.rs:936-1029). final_events and backfill_snapshots widen local IDs only when multiple event PIDs were observed, while correlate_heap_intervals brackets an event between sampled checkpoints; neither backfill nor bracketing fabricates an exact source expression (src/trace.rs:2564-2655). build_heap_state keeps the last bytes previously captured while alive, including on a subsequently freed block, with its original observation stop (src/trace.rs:2658-2715). At a normal terminal boundary verify_event_status checks destructor ACKs and reports absent/damaged transport; the ACK cannot repair missing event lines, and an unobserved forked process is not counted as covered (src/allocation_tracker.rs:178-260, src/trace.rs:477-483,906-943). text linked C call - __wrap_malloc - real malloc: result + raw return PC __wrap_malloc - event file - read_new - parse_event_line: RawEvent(pid,seq,id,...) HeapTimeline::ingest - BlockState + HeapEvent (or failed/incomplete evidence) GDB source stop - push_snapshot: live block bytes - HeapBlockInfo addr2line - apply_caller_locations; final_events - checkpoint interval Source details: allocator runtime(engine-allocator-deep.html), heap reconstruction(engine-heap-deep.html), recorder(engine-recorder-deep.html), GDB reads(engine-gdb-deep.html). D. realloc is a new lifetime only when the event says so Example and transition fixtures/c/heap_provenance_realloc.c:14-45 deliberately contains a 256-to-128 resize, a huge failed resize, a larger resize, realloc(zeroed, 0), and realloc(NULL, 24). These are fixture branches, not guaranteed outcomes on another host: even the variable named same cannot prove same-address reallocation. __wrap_realloc reads its fixed-table predecessor before invoking __real_realloc and emits old_id, old_addr, returned address, new ID and one of new, ok_same, ok_moved, zero or failed (c_runtime/alloc_tracker.c:387-443). For a successful same-address or moved result it allocates a fresh ID and updates the table; failed nonzero resize preserves the original entry. The zero classification describes this runtime's glibc realloc(ptr,0) returning NULL and freeing the old allocation, not a portable C rule. realloc(NULL,n) is classified as new on success or failed on failure (c_runtime/alloc_tracker.c:403-418). parse_event_line materializes the status as RawEvent (src/allocation_tracker.rs:82-159); HeapTimeline::ingest handles each branch differently (src/allocation_tracker.rs:606-699). OkSame retires the old BlockState and adds a linked successor when IDs differ; only historical event lines that reuse the same ID update the existing size in place. OkMoved retires the old block by address/ID and links the new block via realloc_from_id; New with no observed predecessor begins observation without inventing an old lifetime. Failed appends AllocationFailed without retiring the old block; Zero retires an observed old block and appends a terminal reallocation event without a new live block. retire_block updates live-byte usage; add_block rejects invalid or duplicate IDs/addresses and marks the PID incomplete rather than forcing a chain (src/allocation_tracker.rs:758-807). The successor link in HeapBlockInfo comes from reconstructed event IDs, not an assignment in the C file (src/trace.rs:2566-2597,2662-2715). At a subsequent source stop, push_snapshot reads only alive_blocks(pid); thus a failed realloc can leave the original eligible for another stopped read, whereas a terminal-free zero event cannot (src/allocation_tracker.rs:861-873, src/trace.rs:2217-2268). correlate_heap_intervals brackets retained realloc events between checkpoint counts; it does not assign an event to the line of observe(same) or a particular execution of a source call (src/trace.rs:2616-2655). An address reused after freeing, an event gap, or a missing ACK must not upgrade an address candidate to predecessor/origin identity. The historical Stage 1 final audit(../stage1-final-audit.md) reports a 15-event heap_provenance_realloc.c run, but this page does not rerun or generalize its outcomes. text fixture branch - __wrap_realloc - __real_realloc: observed return/status wrapper - event file - RawEvent(old_id,old_addr,id,addr,status) HeapTimeline::ingest: ok_same/ok_moved - retire + linked successor failed - old remains; zero - old retired, no successor GDB checkpoint - alive_blocks - optional stopped-byte HeapBlockInfo final_events/backfill_snapshots - qualified IDs and checkpoint intervals Source details: allocator runtime(engine-allocator-deep.html), heap lifetimes(engine-heap-deep.html), GDB checkpoint(engine-gdb-deep.html), recorder(engine-recorder-deep.html). E. Static metadata meets runtime evidence without becoming execution proof Example and transition fixtures/c/ast_source.c:2-17 contains a TAKE macro, struct Point, several allocator calls on one line, a member assignment, and a shadowed value. These are useful static syntax cases; no AST node, initializer or declaration establishes that a call executed or that bytes were initialized. trace_program_inner calls dwarf::extract_excluding on the GCC debug binary and rejects a registry with no eligible project compilation unit (src/trace.rs:351-367,2731-2759, src/dwarf.rs:578-630). This produces a TypeRegistry of units, type entries and declarations while excluding the injected tracker CU. With clang_ast enabled, clang_ast::analyze separately invokes Clang for bounded user translation units and populates SourceMetadataRegistry with translation-unit statuses, declarations and expressions; rejected flags, unavailable Clang, timeout and partial extraction remain explicit (src/trace.rs:368-391, src/clang_ast.rs:180-225,228-389). Clang parsing is opt-in, and its provider may be incompatible with GCC for cross-provider correlation. Before GDB capture, dwarf::ObservationTypes::new builds declaration/type lookup tables (src/trace.rs:434-437, src/dwarf.rs:879-971). ObservationTypes::enrich attaches type_ref/declaration_ref to a uniquely plausible stopped VariableInfo, possibly supplying a static size only when a runtime extent is absent and storage is known; gdb_mi::capture_state and recorder::capture_global still obtain values, storage and bytes from the stopped inferior (src/dwarf.rs:973-1039, src/gdb_mi.rs:1971-2174, src/recorder.rs:512-647). After heap reconstruction, dwarf::associate matches runtime declarations by recorded full file, declaration line, name and (where available) function; ambiguous or missing matches remain unlinked (src/trace.rs:944-955, src/dwarf.rs:1042-1102). clang_ast::correlate_declarations separately matches AST to DWARF by name/location/kind with a restricted missing-column fallback (src/clang_ast.rs:832-945). Finally evidence::fuse runs once, without new GDB queries, after runtime observations and heap history exist (src/trace.rs:966-968, src/evidence/mod.rs:33-90). declarations::link_source_members and source_links::link_expressions add eligible member/type references; source_links::link_runtime bridges an observed variable to an AST declaration only through the same unique DWARF declaration ID (src/evidence/mod.rs:56-74, src/evidence/source_links.rs:15-143). heap::correlate delegates to clang_ast::correlate_heap_calls: a unique direct compatible call on a resolved file/line is a candidate, while multiple or macro-expanded calls are ambiguities, never exact event-to-expression execution (src/evidence/heap.rs:8-10, src/clang_ast.rs:947-1053). validation::audit removes dangling newly constructed references, and EvidenceFusionSummary counts retained links/rejections (src/evidence/validation.rs:15-180, src/evidence/mod.rs:77-90). With no static provider fusion stays absent; with AST off, DWARF-only enrichment remains possible but no AST source-expression bridge exists. text GCC debug ELF - extract_excluding - TypeRegistry - ObservationTypes optional Clang source pass - analyze - SourceMetadataRegistry GDB stop - capture_state/ObservationTypes::enrich - VariableInfo + bytes finished heap + snapshots - dwarf::associate - declaration_ref AST/DWARF location match - evidence::fuse - qualified links/candidates validation::audit - cleared invalid links + EvidenceFusionSummary Source details: DWARF(engine-dwarf-deep.html), Clang AST(engine-ast-deep.html), evidence fusion(engine-fusion-deep.html), stack observations(engine-stack-deep.html). F. A fatal stop or timeout retains evidence without claiming a normal exit Example and transition fixtures/c/phase8r3_crash.c:1-3 writes through a volatile null pointer while referring to observed_global; it illustrates the fatal-stop path and requested-global capture. fixtures/c/infinite_loop.c:5-12 illustrates an alternative step/deadline path. These are distinct possible executions, not a combined trace; the historical audit reports a fatal-stop fixture and a step-limit fixture, but neither was rerun here (historical audit(../stage1-final-audit.md)). run_gdb_phase classifies a reported fatal signal after ingesting event lines; classify_signal treats SIGSEGV and other configured fatal signals differently from resource and benign signals (src/trace.rs:1371-1551,2031-2063). It calls capture_or_empty, push_snapshot and capture_requested_globals even at the fatal stop, enriches the snapshot, records a checkpoint if space remains, then constructs CrashReport from observed signal/frame/backtrace via crash_from and sets ExecutionStatus::Crashed (src/trace.rs:1441-1518,2489-2508). A snapshot-cap failure is recorded as truncation; it does not erase the observed crash. exited-signalled/SIGKILL instead records interruption without inventing a cause (src/trace.rs:1423-1440). If an execution command times out waiting for stopped, stop_wait_timeout_status maps that to Timeout; a command-reply timeout before the stage deadline can instead be DebuggerFailure and poison the MI session (src/trace.rs:1754-1797,2069-2089, src/gdb_mi.rs:583-609). The loop also checks source checkpoint, step, instruction, command, output and wall budgets (src/trace.rs:1569-1575,1682-1729,1932-1953). For a nonterminal limit/deadline it kills the inferior tree and marks recording gaps/truncation; normal/crash paths terminate through the other branch (src/trace.rs:1954-2024). A final event read can preserve post-stop events, but verify_event_status and HeapHistoryCoverage explicitly flag missing terminal ACKs or incomplete event transport: a crash generally has no destructor ACK, so observed prefix events do not imply complete heap history (c_runtime/alloc_tracker.c:319-336, src/trace.rs:477-483,851-943). trace_program_inner maps the phase status to debugger/tracker StageResult, ExecutionOutcome, resource counters and CrashReport (src/trace.rs:484-588,1007-1065). On a crash with a successful sanitized build and matching trigger, run_sanitizer_pass executes the separate ASan/UBSan binary before Valgrind; otherwise OnCrashOrValgrindError can wait for Valgrind findings (src/trace.rs:49-106,644-680,787-848, src/sanitizer.rs:21-79). matches_crash checks actual native source sites before labeling sanitizer reproduction; different-site findings become diagnostic_observed (src/trace.rs:68-86, src/sanitizer.rs:162-185). valgrind::run_valgrind is another independent process with passive wrapper telemetry and XML diagnostics, never the primary GDB execution (src/trace.rs:682-785, src/valgrind.rs:39-132). Missing tools, expired deadlines or malformed XML are stage failures/skips, not clean analyses. The CLI's json_export::export_json_cancellable separately preflights serialized size and may fail export even when a partial trace exists in memory (src/main.rs:34-78, src/json_export.rs:72-75,139-167). text GDB stop - run_gdb_phase: fatal signal / limit / stop-wait timeout fatal - capture_or_empty - push_snapshot + globals - crash_from: Crashed nonterminal timeout/limit - kill + recorder gap: partial recording final event read - verify_event_status - qualified HeapHistoryCoverage trace_program_inner - optional separate sanitizer / Valgrind executions trace_program_inner - DebugSessionTrace - export_json_cancellable (or export error) Source details: GDB failure paths(engine-gdb-deep.html), diagnostics(engine-diagnostics-deep.html), supervision(engine-supervision-deep.html), recorder(engine-recorder-deep.html), export(engine-export-deep.html). Diagram notes Walkthrough A diagram {{diagram:d2-story-compile}} Configuration to GCC artifacts. Walkthrough B diagram {{diagram:d2-story-checkpoint}} An observed MI stop to a retained checkpoint. Walkthrough C diagram {{diagram:d2-story-malloc}} A wrapped allocation to reconstructed lifetime evidence. Walkthrough D diagram {{diagram:d2-story-realloc}} Recorded realloc statuses to branch-specific transitions. Walkthrough E diagram {{diagram:d2-story-static}} Static declaration metadata to qualified additive references. Walkthrough F diagram {{diagram:d2-story-failure}} A crash or limit through partial evidence and optional separate diagnostics.

title: Source file handbook
summary: 37 · Trace Engine source file handbook In one sentence: This is a reading guide for engine source files, not a claim that you need to understand every helper before using the trace. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Orchestrator
text: 37 · Trace Engine source file handbook In one sentence: This is a reading guide for engine source files, not a claim that you need to understand every helper before using the trace. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Orchestrator Code such as trace.rs that decides which stage runs next and handles its result. File chapter A focused explanation of the responsibilities and limitations of one source file. Example. Start with trace.rs to see the big sequence, then visit gdb_mi.rs if your question is about debugger replies, or allocation_tracker.rs if it is about heap events. What not to assume: Source file order is not the same as runtime execution order, especially for optional or failed stages. The big picture This is the coverage index for the DOC-2 engine handbook. Each row names a production Stage 1 file, its ownership boundary, and the detailed chapter that explains its types, functions, state and failure behavior. The function reference(engine-functions.html) is generated from reviewed graph nodes; the complete lexical symbol index remains in functions(functions.html). How to use the handbook Start with entry and orchestration(engine-entry-deep.html), then follow the execution path through compilation, GDB/MI, stopped-state capture, heap reconstruction, static metadata, diagnostics and export. A file's presence here means it has a detailed chapter; it does not mean every private helper has an independently reviewed walkthrough. Source locations are from the inspected worktree, not a claim that historical line numbers remain stable. Engine files and detailed treatment Production file Responsibility Detailed treatment --------- src/main.rs CLI process entry, exit codes and final export call Entry and errors(engine-entry-deep.html) src/lib.rs Crate module declarations and public re-exports Entry and errors(engine-entry-deep.html) src/cli.rs Clap arguments, config merge and source validation Entry and errors(engine-entry-deep.html) src/config.rs Build, trace and sanitizer request types/defaults Entry and errors(engine-entry-deep.html) src/error.rs Engine error taxonomy and result alias Entry and errors(engine-entry-deep.html) src/compiler.rs GCC argv, probes, builds and diagnostic normalization Compiler internals(engine-compiler-deep.html) src/trace.rs Session orchestration, stop loop, assembly and caller resolution GDB controller(engine-gdb-deep.html) src/gdb_mi.rs GDB/MI2 process, command tokens, reader tasks and state capture GDB controller(engine-gdb-deep.html) src/mi_parser.rs GDB/MI lexer and typed record parser MI2 parser(engine-mi-deep.html) src/recorder.rs Resident observations, checkpoints, instructions and journal append Recorder(engine-recorder-deep.html) src/memory.rs Process maps, pointer extents and address-candidate qualification Stack and memory(engine-stack-deep.html) src/dwarf.rs GCC ELF/DWARF registry, origin resolution and observation types DWARF extraction(engine-dwarf-deep.html) src/clang_ast.rs Optional Clang JSON syntax extraction and source correlation Clang AST(engine-ast-deep.html) src/allocation_tracker.rs C runtime writer, event reader, heap timeline and caller resolution Heap reconstruction(engine-heap-deep.html) c_runtime/alloc_tracker.c Linked malloc/calloc/realloc/free wrappers and event/ACK files C allocator runtime(engine-allocator-deep.html) src/valgrind.rs Independent Memcheck process, XML parsing and ID-free site candidates Valgrind and sanitizers(engine-diagnostics-deep.html) src/sanitizer.rs title: Algorithms & invariants
summary: 38 · Algorithms and invariants In one sentence: An algorithm is the rule the code follows. An invariant is a condition the code tries to keep true while following that rule. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Invariant A checkabl
text: 38 · Algorithms and invariants In one sentence: An algorithm is the rule the code follows. An invariant is a condition the code tries to keep true while following that rule. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Invariant A checkable rule, such as 'a later recorded stop must not be relabeled as an earlier one.' Bounded A request is limited by time, record count or bytes, and the limitation is reported rather than silently ignored. Example. When a GDB step times out, the algorithm records that failure instead of turning the attempted instruction into a completed instruction. This preserves the invariant that attempts and completions are different. What not to assume: A proof about an algorithm under recorded inputs is not a promise that external tools never fail or that all processes were observed. The big picture This page collects the mechanisms that are easy to misread from a single function name: supervised process control, MI dispatch, stop classification, bounded capture, DWARF reference chasing, source correlation, heap prefix reconstruction, fusion auditing and export preflight. Each section names the state that makes the algorithm correct and the evidence it refuses to invent. Supervised bounded subprocesses supervisor::output starts an owned process group, drains stdout and stderr concurrently into separate bounded buffers, and waits for both the direct child and pipe EOF (src/supervisor.rs:226-304). It does not let a successful parent hide a descendant holding a pipe open. On cancellation or deadline it terminates the group, reaps what it can, and gives unfinished pipes a short bounded drain. ProcessOutput.output_truncated is a capture fact, not permission to claim complete diagnostics (src/supervisor.rs:200-304). The invariant is deadline plus ownership, not a sandbox. A compiler or diagnostic stage can time out after producing useful bytes; those bytes remain partial evidence. A later stage must not infer success from the earlier stage's retained prefix. MI tokens and asynchronous stops A command receives a monotonically increasing token. GdbSession::execute registers a pending waiter, writes a tokened MI command to stdin, and waits for the matching ^ result. The stdout reader task parses complete records and routes tokened results separately from asynchronous stopped records (src/gdb_mi.rs:532-671,2302-2484). This separation is the central correctness rule: -exec-step-instruction returning ^done means the command was accepted, not that the next stop was observed. The reader preserves unknown classes and nested tuple/list structure through mi_parser; a malformed or partial line is an error/diagnostic, never a fabricated stopped frame (src/mi_parser.rs:53-205,396-636). Cancellation and EOF can leave a pending command unresolved; the caller must treat that as no sufficient completion evidence. Stop-loop classification and checkpoints At each observed stop, run_gdb_phase first ingests available complete heap rows, then classifies the stop. A fatal signal, an exit, a normal source change and a dual-mode instruction attempt are different branches (src/trace.rs:1371-1568,1720-1929). The frame PC at a stop is the next address; an instruction event stores the pre-attempt PC plus the next observed address and stop reason. An absent after-stop is not proof that the attempted instruction completed. Source checkpoints are retained when the implementation's source/origin and change rules select them. Repeated loop lines can remain distinct events. A checkpoint's instruction_position counts attempts before that snapshot; it is not an allocation timestamp or an exact instruction index into an unrecorded interval. Bounded stopped-state and memory capture gdb_mi::capture_state builds a CapturedState from the selected frame, bounded frame-zero locals/arguments, optional caller frames, globals and memory requests (src/gdb_mi.rs:1840-2227). recorder::capture_variable_memory performs bounded inferior reads and retains raw bytes plus readability/truncation status (src/recorder.rs:45-185). A variable's static type from DWARF can supply a fallback extent only when the runtime extent is absent and the type is known; GDB remains the source of live values (src/dwarf.rs:973-1040). The capture invariant is preserve the observation, including its failure. A missing read or an over-budget object remains visible as unavailable/partial; captured bytes do not prove initialization or an active union member. Pointer enrichment compares addresses with observed maps and heap extents, producing candidates, not ownership proofs (src/memory.rs:141-205). DWARF origin and specification resolution OriginResolver follows DW_AT_specification or DW_AT_abstract_origin, filling only missing name/location/type attributes. A UnitRef stays in the current CU; an absolute DebugInfoRef is mapped through an index of absolute DIE offsets to its owning CU header (src/dwarf.rs:213-423,535-575). The visited set is (CU header offset, unit DIE offset), with a four-hop limit and cycle detection. The invariant is bounded reference identity. A missing target, unsupported form or cycle becomes an unresolved limitation; it does not fall back to a same-name declaration in another translation unit. CU-qualified keys preserve distinct declarations that happen to share a basename or symbol spelling. Clang spans and heap-call candidates span computes source byte offsets and rejects zero/out-of-range or included-header locations; macro expansions retain a separate spelling location (src/clang_ast.rs:397-488). correlate_heap_calls indexes retained direct and macro allocator calls by canonical file and covered line, then accepts only a unique direct compatible call on a resolved return-address-minus-one line. Multiple calls or macro-only calls become explicit ambiguities (src/clang_ast.rs:947-1054). The invariant is site-only candidacy. A resolved line chooses neither a particular dynamic call nor an allocation ID. An AST declaration/expression ID is static syntax identity, never a runtime activation identity. Heap verified prefixes and realloc state EventFileReader accepts only complete newline-terminated rows; parse_event_line requires the exact 10-field or calloc 12-field shape (src/allocation_tracker.rs:82-160,262-400). HeapTimeline::ingest requires per-PID sequences to start at 1 and increase by one. A gap or malformed transport marks that PID/global history incomplete; later rows remain available but cannot retroactively certify missing transitions (src/allocation_tracker.rs:521-756). Realloc is a branch table, not pointer arithmetic: failure preserves the old block; same-address success retires and recreates a linked lifetime; moved success links a successor; terminal zero-size free retires without a successor (src/allocation_tracker.rs:606-699). JSON IDs are widened to (pid << 32) local_id only when multiple event PIDs were observed, with overflow reported rather than silently colliding (src/allocation_tracker.rs:897-921). Fusion and construction-time audit evidence::fuse runs once after runtime and heap records exist. It indexes DWARF declarations/types, links AST fields and expressions only through unique CU/DIE-compatible matches, bridges runtime variables only through an already exact DWARF declaration ID, and delegates heap-call candidacy to the AST matcher (src/evidence/mod.rs:33-91). The final audit removes dangling references and verifies member name plus byte offset (src/evidence/validation.rs:15-197). The invariant is additive, qualified references. Fusion does not rewrite observed values, addresses, activation IDs or allocation lifetimes, and it does not promote a source candidate to execution proof. Exact JSON preflight serialize_limited writes through a byte-counting writer and rejects output above the configured cap before the destination is committed. For a file, export_json serializes to a sibling temporary file, flushes and renames it, then serializes to stdout (src/json_export.rs:9-168). The budget is per serialized JSON document, not a bound on the already assembled trace or on arbitrary serializer memory. The invariant is no partial final JSON from a known size violation. A late stdout error after a successful rename is an operational failure with a committed file, not a rollback; a capped capture journal is a different, earlier boundary. Where to read next Use the source handbook(engine-handbook.html) for file-by-file ownership, the function reference(engine-functions.html) for reviewed call relationships, and the walkthroughs(engine-walkthroughs.html) for six subsystem-level sequences. The limitations(limitations.html) page is part of every algorithm claim.

summary: 39 · Trace Engine function reference In one sentence: Use this reference when you already have a function name and want to find its purpose, source and reviewed connections. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Signature The functi
text: 39 · Trace Engine function reference In one sentence: Use this reference when you already have a function name and want to find its purpose, source and reviewed connections. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Signature The function name, inputs and output written in source code. Reviewed graph entry A function whose purpose and linked relationships were checked against source instead of guessed from its name. Example. Look up run_gdb_phase, then follow its links to the stop loop. The entry tells you where to read, while the debugger chapter explains what the stop actually means. What not to assume: A direct source call may be conditional. The catalog does not prove that it executed in a particular trace. The big picture This page lists the engine functions that have a reviewed entry in the DOC-2 call-flow graph. Each entry shows the actual source location, signature, purpose, input/output boundary, qualification, and classified incoming/outgoing relationships. Use the subsystem links to read the surrounding algorithm and state transitions. Scope and reading order A reviewed entry is not a claim that the function ran in a particular trace. Direct edges were checked at call expressions; subprocess, data and conceptual edges retain their own labels. For functions absent here, search the complete function index(functions.html), then consult the file chapter in the source handbook(engine-handbook.html). DOC-2 prioritizes orchestration, debugger, compiler, heap, metadata, diagnostics and export paths; not every private helper is expanded yet. This distinction is intentional: an accurate inventory is more useful than a large but unsupported function encyclopedia. title: Trace data model
summary: 40 · DebugSessionTrace · the recorded data model In one sentence: The data model is the shape of the saved recording. Think of it as labeled folders, not a reconstruction of missing history. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Sna
text: 40 · DebugSessionTrace · the recorded data model In one sentence: The data model is the shape of the saved recording. Think of it as labeled folders, not a reconstruction of missing history. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Snapshot One saved view at a debugger pause: where the program stopped, what variables were read, and what heap blocks were observed. Optional field A value that can be missing because the tool did not record or could not establish it; missing is not automatically false. Example. A trace may contain a variable's displayed value but no raw bytes, or a heap event with no source location. Both can be valid partial evidence if the missing part is kept visible. What not to assume: A shortened JSON field example on this page illustrates the schema; it is not a complete file you can import. Level 1 · Intuition A trace is not a video of a program. It is a set of timestamped/stopped observations, bounded attempts and gaps, heap telemetry, optional static metadata and diagnostics. Links between them use different identity domains. Preserving absent evidence is just as important as preserving a successful read. {{diagram:records}} Level 2 · Record relationships Picture the JSON as a notebook with several sections written at different times. In Rust, DebugSessionTrace holds the notebook; RecordingData is folded into the top-level JSON, so Rust's recording.instruction_events appears as JSON's instruction_events. Each source_checkpoints entry points to a saved snapshot by array position, not by including a second snapshot copy. disassembly_table is a dictionary of instructions; a saved instruction event refers to a dictionary entry by instruction_id. Running the same instruction three times still gives three separate events. trace_gaps mark intervals without exact captured events. Heap events list observed operations in time order; allocation_lifetimes describe a block's start and end; heap_state describes saved block state. They answer different questions. Instruction coverage, heap heap_history, journal storage and the outcomes in stage_results can be complete or partial independently. Events, gaps and checkpoints - snapshotsi.step_index=i: captured checkpoint position. snapshotsi.observation.stop_id: processed debugger stop counter; may have holes. instruction_position: number of attempts preceding it. - instruction_eventsj.event_id: ordered attempted instruction ID; optional checkpoint_id references a recent snapshot, not an exact temporal join. stop_id_before/after refer to debugger observations. - trace_gapsk.instruction_position is a boundary where instructions were not captured; its unknown instruction count is never guessed. Variables, bytes and heap VariableInfo.read_status, bytes_status and memory_evidence describe distinct observations. Pointer address is storage and points_to is the pointee. HeapEvent.sequence is per-PID, not event-vector position. HeapBlockInfo.observed_at_stop timestamps heap byte reads; a freed final block may retain historical bytes. AllocationLifetime has an allocation sequence and optional free sequence; a successful realloc can link old and new lifetime IDs. The schema does not create pointer origin from address equality. Level 3 · Actual schema excerpt and paths rust // Reduced field excerpt from src/models.rs; other fields omitted. pub struct DebugSessionTrace { pub schema_version: u32, pub snapshots: Vec<ExecutionSnapshot, pub heap_events: Vec<HeapEvent, pub heap_state: Vec<HeapBlockInfo, pub execution_status: ExecutionStatus, pub stage_results: StageResults, // serde(flatten) pub recording: RecordingData, } Illustrative reduced excerpt, not a copy/paste Rust definition or complete JSON: DebugSessionTrace also contains typed execution_limits, execution, compilation results, optional metadata and reports, usage and notes. For the actual declaration, see src/models.rs::DebugSessionTrace and schema reference(schema.html). json {"schema_version":2,"execution_status":"step_limit_reached","instruction_count":203,"coverage":{"scope":"user_code","complete_for_scope":false,"truncation_reasons":"max_steps"}} This is an illustrative partial JSON projection: no unspecified keys are implied, and a real trace's truncation-reason list may include additional causes. The importer requires the full model, not this excerpt. schema_version is 2 for supported V2.1/V2.2 documents; a missing marker defaults to 2, but unknown old execution_limits fields can still make pre-V2.1 files fail to deserialize. See TP-1 compatibility(parser-ingestion.htmllevel-2-architecture-and-compatibility). NOTE: The wire model records uncertainty as Option/nullable values and explicit status fields. Never rewrite a missing stop_id_after, unloaded AST registry or unreadable bytes to a successful observation. Find identity semantics in the reference dictionary(schema.htmlidentity-domains).

title: TP-1 · Load & compatibility
summary: 41 · TP-1 · Loading traces without inventing data In one sentence: Opening a trace is like opening a notebook: check that it is the right kind of notebook before relying on what its pages claim. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------
text: 41 · TP-1 · Loading traces without inventing data In one sentence: Opening a trace is like opening a notebook: check that it is the right kind of notebook before relying on what its pages claim. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Schema The agreed JSON field format. Stage 1 uses schema version 2 for supported V2.1 and V2.2 recordings. JSONL One JSON object per line. The runtime journal is not the final trace document and cannot reconstruct missing reports. Example. TraceStore::open can read a well-formed old_id=7. That still does not prove allocation 7 is the right predecessor; only deeper validation can examine the supporting events. What not to assume: An unsupported older example or malformed input fails import. A supported but incomplete trace may load and remain incomplete. Level 1 · Intuition The Trace Parser reads the engine's finished JSON exactly once and makes a single immutable TraceStore available to multiple readers. Successful parsing means schema-compatible, not “all records are internally consistent” and not “the program ran to completion.” Deep validation is an explicit separate step. {{diagram:ownership}} Level 2 · Architecture and compatibility TraceStore::open(path, options) first checks how many bytes it is allowed to read. It reads one byte past the configured maximum only to tell the difference between an exactly fitting file and an oversized one. Next it distinguishes a complete JSON trace from a JSONL journal. from_reader and from_json_bytes accept input supplied by Rust code instead of a file. from_trace accepts a trace that Rust has already decoded, but checks only its schema version, not the truth of its relationships. Default import limits are 512 MiB of input and 2,000,000 JSONL records; oversized input is rejected, not quietly cut off. After loading, TraceStore keeps a shared Arc for the one original trace and another for its position indexes. Cloning the store shares these rather than duplicating every snapshot. The supported format uses schema_version=2. The six supported V2.1 examples still load, even when newer optional fields were never recorded. In this model, a missing schema marker is interpreted as version 2. That does not mean every older file works: four pre-V2.1 examples/v2_.json files use a removed limit field and cannot be decoded. Wrong schema, bad text encoding, broken JSON and oversized input each produce a specific error. By contrast, a C program crashing, timing out or reaching its step limit can produce a valid but partial trace; those outcomes are not reasons to pretend the JSON is malformed. JSONL is not a TraceStore The parse_journal family can read each JSONL line as a configuration, checkpoint, allocation, gap, instruction or other recorded item. It also says whether the last line was torn off and whether the journal was finalized. A partially written last line can be identified as partial; a completely written but malformed line is an error. Why not just open the journal as a trace? The final heap state, crash reports and other end-of-session results may never have been written to it. TraceStore::open therefore refuses to guess a complete trace from journal lines. See storage and limits(engine-limits.html). Level 3 · Implementation and API rust use c_trace_engine::trace_parser::{TraceLoadOptions, TraceStore}; fn main() - Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error { let store = TraceStore::open("examples/v21_dual.json", TraceLoadOptions::default())?; assert_eq!(store.trace().schema_version, 2); let validated = store.validated_semantic(); // opt-in; not part of open() if !validated.report().is_structurally_sound() { eprintln!("import has contradictory record relationships"); } Ok(()) } The snippet is executable as a Rust example in this crate (adjust the path if run elsewhere); for a larger end-to-end query see Practical usage(usage.htmllevel-3-load-and-validate). Actual TraceStore methods: open, from_reader, from_json_bytes, from_trace, trace, shared, source, validate_deep. src/trace_parser/{mod,json,journal,error}.rs implement ingestion; TraceParseError covers malformed input, unsupported schema, journal-only input and limits. src/trace_parser/indexes.rs eagerly builds positions after successful decoding. open preserves file path/byte length in a small TraceSourceMetadata descriptor. WARNING: Neither schema compatibility nor heap_process_scope() on raw input certifies a claimed relationship. For imported/untrusted data, inspect validated.report() and the confidence/coverage of each relationship before presenting it as fact.

title: TP-2 · Position indexes
summary: 42 · TP-2 · Compact, position-only indexes In one sentence: The parser keeps an index the way a book keeps page numbers. It does not photocopy every page of the book. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Position index A small tabl
text: 42 · TP-2 · Compact, position-only indexes In one sentence: The parser keeps an index the way a book keeps page numbers. It does not photocopy every page of the book. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Position index A small table that says which position in the original trace array contains a record you asked for. Borrowed result A view of the existing saved record, not a newly invented or copied instruction event. Example. If allocation 7 has events at positions 2 and 10, the index stores those two positions. A query uses them to return the original events, in their recorded order. What not to assume: An index lets you find a record quickly; it cannot prove that a recorded relationship is correct. Level 1 · Intuition A large trace repeats instruction addresses and source lines thousands of times. Scanning every event for each question would waste time; copying every record into lookup tables would waste memory. TP-2 builds keys → integer positions once and borrows original records when queried. It does not create an address→allocation provenance index. {{diagram:ownership}} Level 2 · What is indexed When TraceStore is created, TraceIndexes::build makes lookup tables once. ExecutionsIndex answers “at which saved event positions did instruction 12 appear?” It keeps a compact range of position numbers for each compiled instruction. SourceIndex answers “which recorded events had this exact file path and line?” It also lets you go back from an instruction to recorded source positions. AllocationIndex answers “where are the events, final block and lifetime for allocation ID 7?” MetadataIndex locates DWARF and Clang source/type records by their IDs. These tables store numbers and keys, not second copies of instruction events, snapshots or raw bytes. If you already have a snapshot's vector position, the parser can look it up directly. Other questions, such as “which snapshot has GDB stop ID 17?”, use a fast binary search only after checking that the imported stop IDs are in order. A broken order produces OrderingViolation, not a guessed answer. To show heap events between two saved snapshots, the parser uses their recorded running event counts. If an intermediate stop was never saved, that interval is only an approximate time window: it does not prove the event happened at the later stop. The index never treats equal filename endings or matching addresses as proven identities. Mini example Disassembly instruction 12 may occur at instruction_events positions 5, 21, 36. The index contains three u32 positions, not three copies of the event or one merged “executed once” record. instruction_execution_positions(12) returns that slice; instruction_executions(12) borrows canonical event records at each position. instruction_id=12 is not event 12. Level 3 · Source and query contracts - src/trace_parser/indexes.rs::{TraceIndexes, ExecutionsIndex, SourceIndex, AllocationIndex, MetadataIndex, OrderingFacts}. - TraceStore::{instruction_event, instruction_range, events_at_checkpoint, snapshot_at_stop, instruction_executions, executed_events_for_source, heap_events_for_allocation, allocation_lifetime} in src/trace_parser/mod.rs. rust let positions: &u32 = store.heap_event_positions_for_allocation(allocation_id); for &position in positions { let heap_event = &store.heap_events()position as usize; assert_eq!(heap_event.allocation_id, allocation_id); } This excerpt assumes store and allocation_id are defined. It visits recorded heap-event positions without confusing them with event_id, stop IDs or allocation IDs; the executable usage sample(usage.htmlcheckpoints-and-paging) also handles empty traces and paginates. TraceIndexes::estimated_bytes() is a rough logical estimate of index structures, not process RSS. In the Stage 1 audit the 900-snapshot/3,143-instruction trace had ~28,369 estimated index bytes, ~1.13 ms median index build and ~17 MiB parser-process RSS after indexing (process includes trace, runtime and buffers; workload-specific). NOTE: A valid empty source/heap lookup means “no matching recorded item”; it is not a statement that nothing happened in a gap, another process or an uninstrumented library.

title: TP-3 · Borrowed views
summary: 43 · TP-3 · Borrowed views and EvidenceRef In one sentence: A view is a convenient way to look at the trace you already loaded. It does not own a second independent history. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Arc Rust's shared-ow
text: 43 · TP-3 · Borrowed views and EvidenceRef In one sentence: A view is a convenient way to look at the trace you already loaded. It does not own a second independent history. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Arc Rust's shared-ownership handle: several readers can refer to the same underlying saved trace without copying all its records. EvidenceRef A citation to one original record, tied to the trace it came from. Example. Two readers cloned from one TraceStore can resolve the same citation. If you independently load the same JSON again, its references belong to a different trace owner and are rejected as foreign. What not to assume: A borrowed view cannot recreate a value the engine never captured. Level 1 · Intuition One large immutable trace should have many lightweight readers, not many copies. A view is a borrowed window into canonical records; an EvidenceRef is a trace-scoped citation that can later be resolved against that same recording. Equal numeric indices in two independent traces do not refer to the same execution. {{diagram:ownership}} Level 2 · Ownership and lifecycle TraceStore holds two shared Rust Arc values: the original DebugSessionTrace and the small TraceIndexes. You can clone the store without copying the trace. raw() offers recorded items directly. semantic_input() opens a borrowed CheckpointContext for a saved snapshot, so callers can inspect its current frame, optional callers, globals and observed heap without taking ownership of their bytes. events_at_checkpoint() uses recorded checkpoint tags, while a heap-event interval uses counts from neighboring saved snapshots. If the trace has no supported stop or source association, the query says Unavailable; it does not add a stop to make an answer look complete. EvidenceLocation is like a precise address inside the notebook: “snapshot 3, variable 1,” or “heap event at array position 7.” EvidenceRef adds a weak link to which loaded notebook it came from. When you resolve the reference, the parser checks that owner first. A cloned TraceStore points to the same trace and accepts it; opening the same JSON independently creates a new owner and returns ForeignTrace. This prevents accidentally linking events from two separate loads just because their numbers happen to match. An EvidenceRef is not a portable ID you can serialize and use against another trace. Worked citation A variable on the top frame of snapshot 3 may be observed with snapshot.context.variable_evidence(1)?. Resolving that reference returns the same canonical VariableInfo as store.trace().snapshots3.variables1. A later stop with a local of the same name is not substituted. See TP-6 variable confidence(parser-semantic.htmlpointer-and-memory-confidence). Level 3 · APIs and errors rust use c_trace_engine::trace_parser::{EvidenceLocation, TraceStore}; let store = TraceStore::open("examples/v21_dual.json", Default::default())?; let cite = store.evidence_ref(EvidenceLocation::Snapshot(0))?; let same_run = store.resolve_evidence(&cite)?; // borrows original record let _ = (cite.location(), same_run); The snippet is a body excerpt (wrap it in fn main() - Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error); see Practical usage(usage.htmllevel-3-load-and-validate) for a standalone example. Implementation: src/trace_parser/{views,evidence}.rs; TraceStore::raw, semantic_input, evidence_ref, resolve_evidence. A QueryError distinguishes OutOfRange, InvalidRange, LimitExceeded, InvalidReference, ForeignTrace, Unavailable and OrderingViolation. No caller should turn an error into “zero evidence.” NOTE: A borrowed CheckpointContext cannot outlive its store. Keeping a separate Arc<DebugSessionTrace alive is possible with shared(), but a different TraceStore::open still has a different trace identity even with byte-identical contents.

title: TP-5 · Deep validation
summary: 44 · TP-5 · Deep structural validation In one sentence: A file can be readable JSON and still tell an impossible story. Validation asks whether its records agree, without demanding that every possible event was observed. Key terms
text: 44 · TP-5 · Deep structural validation In one sentence: A file can be readable JSON and still tell an impossible story. Validation asks whether its records agree, without demanding that every possible event was observed. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Structural corruption A contradiction: for example, a claimed realloc predecessor conflicts with the recorded creation event. Partial coverage A legitimate missing stretch, such as a crash or exhausted recording limit. Partial does not automatically mean corrupt. Example. If a trace reports a block came from realloc of ID 7, validation checks the old and new events, PID and lifetimes. If those contradict, do not display the link as certain, even though the raw field is preserved. What not to assume: TraceStore::open checks the format. Call validated_semantic() or deep validation explicitly for relationship checks. Level 1 · Intuition A JSON file can have the right shape and still contradict itself. TP-5's opt-in deep validation checks cross-record relationships. It distinguishes a corrupt link from a legitimate missing observation: a crashed or truncated program can yield a structurally sound but incomplete trace. {{diagram:confidence}} Level 2 · Architecture validate_deep() runs a list of consistency checks and collects the results in a ValidationReport. Each finding says where a problem was found, what kind it was, and how often it occurred. There are four important kinds: StructuralCorruption means records contradict one another; PartialCoverage means some intended observations are missing; UnavailableEvidence means a particular link cannot be supported; OptionalAbsence means an optional source of information is not there. is_structurally_sound() means there was no contradiction. It does not promise that all instructions, processes or bytes were captured. is_partial() asks a separate question about missing coverage. TP-6 runs this check once when you ask for its validated view. If structural contradictions exist, it refuses to give definite semantic confidence, while leaving raw records visible for investigation. The checks ask practical questions: Do referenced snapshots and instructions exist? Are recorded stops in the required order? Do the counts agree? Are two different heap blocks claiming the same lifetime ID? Does a pointer marked address_only incorrectly claim a definite allocation origin? Does a trace claim all child processes were observed without evidence? The validator also checks static metadata links and whether reports agree with their stated coverage. For example, a pointer address inside block 7 is not enough to justify a claim that block 7 created that pointer. Older traces may simply lack a provenance or process-scope field: that means unavailable, not “the parser has filled it in.” Realloc link verification A block's realloc_from_id is not enough. realloc_link compares indexed creation events of both new and predecessor identities with lifetimes: Reallocated must name the exact old ID; PID, order, allocation/free sequence and direction must agree. Self-links, cycles and explicitly conflicting events are structural contradictions even if history is partial. Missing corroboration receives UnavailableEvidence; an observed link in incomplete scope cannot become definite. glibc's realloc(ptr,0) terminal-free same-ID/null-address/zero-size event ends a lifetime but is not new lifetime creation. No address equality decides a predecessor. Heap lifetimes(engine-heap.html) explains the source events. Level 3 · Report and import example rust let store = TraceStore::open(path, TraceLoadOptions::default())?; let report = store.validate_deep(); // explicit; not called by TraceStore::open for finding in report.findings() { eprintln!("{} at {}: {}", finding.code, finding.location, finding.detail); } if report.is_partial() { / retain the usable prefix, display missing scope / } This is a body excerpt; use the executable sample(usage.htmllevel-3-load-and-validate) for imports. src/trace_parser/validation.rs::{validate_deep, validate_heap, validate_heap_process_coverage, validate_pointer_reference, realloc_link} implements checks. The resulting ValidationReport borrows no input JSON and aggregates occurrences by code; first_location_findings() on a TP-7 checkpoint is not a completeness proof for that checkpoint. TraceStore::from_trace intentionally remains schema-only. Example findings Code Class Correct response --------- REALLOC_LINK_CONTRADICTORY Structural Preserve raw import for investigation; never claim definite predecessor POINTER_HEAP_PROVENANCE_CONTRADICTORY Structural Do not promote an address-only candidate HEAP_PROCESS_COVERAGE_UNSUPPORTED Structural Reject claimed all-descendant completeness HEAP_HISTORY_INCOMPLETE Partial Preserve observed events; downgrade history-dependent confidence REALLOC_LINK_UNVERIFIED Unavailable Do not infer missing event/lifetime data SANITIZER_REPORT_UNRECORDED Optional Absent report is not proof of no bug WARNING: Trusting successful deserialization—or a raw heap_history.complete field without checking its scope and report—is a false-certainty bug. The F01 regression(../trace-parser-v2.2-repair-f01.md) permanently checks the repaired realloc relationship.

title: TP-6 · Evidence confidence
summary: 45 · TP-6 · Validated semantic evidence In one sentence: A confidence label always describes a particular claim. 'I read these bytes' and 'these bytes were initialized' are not the same claim. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ D
text: 45 · TP-6 · Validated semantic evidence In one sentence: A confidence label always describes a particular claim. 'I read these bytes' and 'these bytes were initialized' are not the same claim. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Definite The named observation or relationship is supported under its stated limits; it does not mean the whole execution was complete. Candidate Evidence fits one explanation, but does not prove it. An address inside a heap block is a candidate for a match, not pointer origin. Example. GDB might definitely have captured four bytes of a pointer. The pointer's allocation origin can still be unavailable, especially if its address was reused. What not to assume: Never promote an AST source call to an executed call, or Valgrind's separate-run address to a primary-run allocation ID. Level 1 · Intuition “Definite” must answer which relationship, in what scope. A readable byte can be a definite capture without a definite C initialization. A pointer can definitely contain an address without a definite allocation origin. TP-6 packages borrowed evidence with per-relationship confidence; it is not the future C Semantic Engine. {{diagram:confidence}} Level 2 · The confidence model Call TraceStore::validated_semantic() once before asking for evidence-level answers. It borrows the unchanged trace and holds the validation report. Each answer has a confidence label. Definite means this specific claim has the required support in its stated scope; Candidate means plausible but unproved; Ambiguous means more than one reading fits; Unavailable means the needed evidence is missing; and Contradictory means recorded facts conflict. A structurally unsound import prevents the semantic layer from calling its relationships definite, but you can still inspect the raw fields to investigate. These labels do not say whether the C program finished, a variable was in scope, its bytes were initialized, or every child was observed: those are different questions. Pointer and memory confidence Ask variable(&EvidenceRef) for the exact local, global or caller variable you want. It points to the saved VariableInfo and any available type information. A pointer's address_candidate means “the number in this pointer could fit in this block's address range.” It does not say the pointer came from that allocation; under the current V2.2 contract, definitive_allocation stays None. If an address was reused or its block already freed, the question can be ambiguous or unavailable. variable_target can find another recorded variable identity at this same stop; it will not search a later stop or a foreign trace, and duplicate identities stay ambiguous. valid_range is merely the number of bytes read at this historical stop. It does not prove those bytes were initialized or still have the same contents later. Identity and source relationships heap(id) brings together the block, its recorded lifetime and events, plus any claimed older realloc ID. The ID's confidence can be definite only for a verified, complete history of the processes actually observed. A realloc relationship needs more: the old and new creation events, PID, order and lifetime boundaries must agree. If an older trace lacks scope details, even a plausible link stays a candidate. source_expression(id) points to an optional Clang description of code that was written, and may show possible heap-call matches. It keeps execution_confidence unavailable: the same source line appearing in an event does not establish which expression ran. Independent diagnostics diagnostics() borrows compile, stage, crash, sanitizer and Valgrind records. valgrind_error(index) exposes source-site candidate confidence, but primary_allocation_id is always None, including for legacy imported raw IDs. process_coverage().unobserved_descendants stays unavailable on sound traces; heap_history.complete is not a descendant census. execution() reports attempted vs retained counts, gaps and engine-declared scope independently. Level 3 · The relevant implementation - src/trace_parser/semantic.rs::{ValidatedSemanticView, EvidenceConfidence, VariableEvidence, MemoryEvidenceView, PointerEvidence, HeapEvidence, SourceExpressionEvidence, ExecutionEvidence, ProcessCoverageEvidence}. - TraceStore::validated_semantic calls self.validate_deep() once. SemanticInputView::validated() offers the same path. self.qualify downgrades on structural unsoundness without mutating source records. - heap(id) uses TP-2's per-allocation event positions and the shared validation::realloc_link classifier. source_expression(id) uses TP-2 metadata candidate/ambiguity positions; no global pointer graph or synthetic execution interpreter is stored. rust let view = store.validated_semantic(); if !view.report().is_structurally_sound() { eprintln!("Structural contradiction; do not present definite links"); } let evidence = view.heap(allocation_id); let _ = (evidence.identity_confidence, evidence.realloc_confidence, evidence.old_id, evidence.events()); This excerpt assumes store and allocation_id; the full runnable walkthrough(usage.htmllevel-3-load-and-validate) covers imports. old_id is raw recorded data and not itself a certified edge; inspect realloc_confidence. A heap-event interval's TP-7 allocation(&view) inherits this same confidence rather than silently upgrading a candidate. WARNING: “Definite” is scoped to the specifically named observation or relationship. It does not imply a complete primary execution, a complete process tree, initialized bytes or that independent diagnostics belong to the primary run.

title: TP-7 · Bounded queries
summary: 46 · TP-7 · Checkpoint composition and bounded pages In one sentence: A checkpoint summary groups related questions about one recorded stop so callers do not have to hunt through unrelated arrays. Key terms Term Plain meaning ----
text: 46 · TP-7 · Checkpoint composition and bounded pages In one sentence: A checkpoint summary groups related questions about one recorded stop so callers do not have to hunt through unrelated arrays. Key terms Term Plain meaning ------ Consumer Code such as a UI or analysis example that asks the parser questions about a trace. Page An explicitly requested slice of results. This API returns at most 128 entries in one request; ask for the next slice if there are more. Example. For a stop with 300 variable records, request positions 0–127, then 128–255, then 256–299. Returning just the first page without saying so would hide evidence. What not to assume: Grouping nearby events is a navigation convenience, not proof that a particular source expression caused one. Level 1 · Intuition A user-facing query often wants several related things at one stop: variables, instruction events, heap events, gaps and optional diagnostics. TP-7 composes existing TP-6 evidence around a checkpoint without copying a trace or inventing a second evidence-ID system. Every page is explicitly limited to 128 records: request the next range to continue. {{diagram:consumer}} Level 2 · What a summary means Start with checkpoint_summary(index) when you know a saved snapshot's position. It keeps a citation to that snapshot and uses the same validated trace. The snapshot position, GDB stop number, instruction-attempt count, PID and source line are different labels; do not substitute one for another. variables_page reads a chosen page of current-frame, global or recorded caller variables with TP-6 confidence. caller_frame and frame_activation describe one actual saved stop, not a lifetime guessed from a function name. instruction_events_page finds events the recording tagged with this checkpoint; that tag helps navigation, but does not prove an expression on the line caused the event. heap_interval_page shows events between two retained snapshots, so the timing is a candidate interval, not an exact stop. Gaps describe attempted-position windows. Optional AST source expressions are only descriptions of written code. Some information belongs to the whole session, not to one stop: overall coverage, compiler and diagnostic reports, Valgrind findings and validation notes. A report first displayed near checkpoint 4 did not necessarily happen because of checkpoint 4. heap_events_page first checks that your allocation citation belongs to this trace, then looks up its numeric ID. When you follow an interval's allocation link, it keeps TP-6's existing realloc confidence rather than quietly changing a candidate into a certainty. Level 3 · Real signatures and bounded traversal rust // Excerpt for a previously constructed view: ValidatedSemanticView. let stop = view.checkpoint_summary(0)?; let len = stop.checkpoint.context.variables().len(); for start in (0..len).step_by(128) { let end = (start + 128).min(len); for item in stop.variables_page(VariableScope::Local, start..end)? { let variable = item?; // borrowed VariableInfo + confidence + EvidenceRef let _ = (variable.info.name.as_str(), variable.value_confidence); } } This excerpt assumes VariableScope is imported and a nonempty trace (use the complete runnable example(usage.htmlcheckpoints-and-paging) for zero-snapshot handling). MAX_CONSUMER_PAGE=128 in src/trace_parser/consumer.rs governs each half-open Range<usize; empty pages are valid. Reversed or past-end ranges return InvalidRange; width 129 returns LimitExceeded without dropping rows. src/trace_parser/indexes.rs supplies event/allocation positions, views.rs supplies borrowed checkpoint context, and semantic.rs supplies unchanged TP-6 confidence. Cost and ordering Stop/event/gap windows use verified order and binary search. Heap interval pagination uses canonical event slices and counters; AST source spans are scanned on demand within bounded registry size. Per-page iteration borrows existing records; it does not build an unbounded output array. The audit exercised 3,143 real retained instructions across 900 checkpoints; separate permanent tests exercise 300 events and 1,024 variables across multiple ≤128 pages. The large real trace does not prove 128 events at a single real checkpoint. See performance(handoff.htmlperformance-not-a-guarantee). NOTE: Keep the page's borrowed lifetime bounded by its ValidatedSemanticView; do not collect an unbounded Vec just because the API makes small pages cheap. When evidence is Unavailable, handle it explicitly rather than displaying an empty success state.
